Constitution The Five Laws · before the document begins
v1.0 · adopted 2026

Five laws. Nothing below overrides them.

Before a single feature is described, we state the five rules the product itself must obey. They are not preferences, not brand language, not marketing pillars. They are constitutional. Every feature in Chapter 10 complies with them. Every ritual in Chapter 11 derives from them. Every monetisation lever in Chapter 13 respects them. If a future idea breaks one of them, the idea is wrong — not the law. This is the contract Archio signs with the trader on his first visit and keeps for the life of the account.

ILaw One
The Spine Law

One record.
All surfaces.

Every act of thinking and every act of doing writes to the same state object. Thesis, confluences, risk budget, cortex reading, verdict — five fields, one record, carried unbroken from analyse to execute to review. The trader’s thinking and his doing are the same object.

No feature is allowed to keep private state that another feature cannot read. No screen is allowed to ask a question already answered on a prior screen.

Enforced By spine/v1 schema
all adapters typed
server audit on every write
IILaw Two
The One-Screen Law

If he must
leave, we failed.

The trader’s canonical act — analyse, forecast, execute, review — takes place on one screen. Tabs are a failure mode. TradingView + Forex Factory + MT5 is a failure mode. Anything that forces a context switch mid-thought is a bug, not a tradeoff.

Every new feature must answer, before it is built: does this let the trader stay on the cockpit, or does it pull him off?

Enforced By F02 cockpit rail
inline copilot
inline execution
IIILaw Three
The Cited Law

Every verdict
shows its work.

No AI output is allowed to appear as an opaque oracle. Every verdict, every scenario, every flag cites its inputs — the rule it checked, the model it ran, the number it read, the timestamp it used. The trader must be able to disagree specifically, not just distrust generally.

Black-box answers are prohibited. The copilot shows the rule, the rule shows the value, the value shows the source. Unbroken.

Enforced By citation object on every verdict
drill-through UI
no unsigned outputs
IVLaw Four
The Auditable Law

What happened
can be proven.

Every trade, every verdict, every rule change, every mentor intervention is immutable, timestamped, and reconstructable. The trader can export his own ledger. A prop firm can verify a challenge without screen-shares. A hedge fund can reconstruct a decision six months later without email forensics.

If it cannot be proven, it did not happen. Receipts, not promises.

Enforced By append-only event log
signed export bundle
public verifier
VLaw Five
The Order Law

Calm is
a feature.

The product’s job is to lower the trader’s heart rate while raising the quality of his decisions. No neon, no gamified streaks, no dark patterns, no dopamine engineering, no confetti on a win, no red shame on a loss. Friction is placed where discipline requires it and removed everywhere else.

The interface should feel like a library after a train station. Silence is the primary animation.

Enforced By motion-reduced by default
no streak mechanics
price shown always
Now, the trader’s version

Five laws, written the way a trader would say them to another trader.

Each stanza below opens with the exact moment the problem happens on a real trading day — the wound the law exists to fix. Then, in plain language, what the rule is and why we refuse to break it. Then, two columns: what you will see in Archio because of this law, and what you will never see, no matter who asks for it, no matter how much they pay.

I
Law One · of Five The Spine Law

One record. All screens.

Your thinking and your trading are the same file. Write it once; it shows up everywhere.

The moment this law exists to fix

It is 07:42 on a Tuesday. You’ve been studying EURUSD for twenty minutes in TradingView. You wrote your thesis in the comment box: London open liquidity sweep below Asian low, then reclaim into FOMC narrative. You circled three confluences — the 4H bullish order block at 1.0820, the daily fib 0.618 at 1.0815, DXY rejecting weekly resistance. You decided on your risk: 0.5% of account, stop below 1.0810, target 1.0860. That is ninety minutes of thinking.

Then you alt-tab to MT5 to actually place the trade, and everything you just thought stays behind in TradingView. MT5 doesn’t know your thesis. It doesn’t know your confluences. It just sees “BUY EURUSD 0.3 lots.” And ninety minutes later, when the trade pulls back scarily into profit, you close at +12 pips — abandoning your +40 target — because your execution screen has no memory of the plan that made +40 the right number. That night, if you journal, you’ll write: “closed early, looked weak.” You will not record that your execution surface forgot why you entered.

The wound — thinking and doing stored in different files.

The law, in plain English

Every thought you put into Archio and every click you make in Archio write to the same file. Not copies. Not sync. Not export. The same object. When you draft a thesis in the Analyze stage, the Forecast stage can already read it. When Forecast runs its scenarios, Execute has them queued. When Execute fires the order, Review has the receipt before the ticker even blinks back. When you write your evening reflection, tomorrow morning’s Analyze stage already has last night’s lesson inside it.

The five fields that live on this one record are: thesis (what you believe), confluences (why you believe it), risk budget (what you’re willing to lose to find out), cortex reading (your state — calm, tilted, tired), and verdict (the AI’s signed opinion on whether to proceed). Five fields. One object. Carried unbroken from the moment you first squint at a chart to the moment you close the position six hours later and write a sentence about it. The trader’s thinking and his doing are the same object.

This is not a technical preference. It is the difference between a platform that makes you better and a platform that makes you tired. A tired trader is a dangerous trader. We refuse to make him tired by asking him to re-explain his plan four times a day to four different screens.

✓In Archio, because of this law
  • Your 07:42 thesis is visible on every screen for the rest of the day — you never re-paste it into a chat to “remind” the AI.
  • If you sized your risk at 0.5% in Analyze, Execute refuses a 1.0% click without a written override.
  • The evening Ledger reads your morning thesis and your execution in the same breath and writes: “you exited +12 vs your +40 target — exit #3 of your 7 Mean-Reversion exits this month.”
  • If you change your mind mid-trade, the amendment is its own stamped event on the same record — not a deletion, not an overwrite.
×Never in Archio, because of this law
  • Opening a second tab to remind yourself what your stop was.
  • An AI assistant that asks “what are you trading today?” at 11 a.m. — it already read your thesis at 07:42.
  • A journal entry that says “I don’t know why I took that trade.” The record itself knows.
  • Re-typing your target and stop into a second screen just to execute the trade.
Enforced by spine/v1 schema · typed adapters on every surface · server-side audit on every write · no feature ships without Spine-compliance review
II
Law Two · of Five The One-Screen Law

If you must leave, we failed.

Everything happens on one screen. Closing a tab to do your job is a design failure.

The moment this law exists to fix

It is 14:55, five minutes before NFP. You are watching DXY on TradingView in one browser tab. Forex Factory is open in a second tab for the red-flag countdown. MT5 is minimized because it’s ugly and you’ll bring it up only when you need it. Your journal is in Notion, in a third tab. Your mentor’s Discord has three unread messages that might be about this release or might be about crypto. Your phone just pinged Myfxbook. Five tabs. Three apps. One trader.

At 14:59:30, DXY starts flushing. You alt-tab. TradingView flashes. Forex Factory counts down. You click into MT5. MT5’s price is a quarter-pip behind TradingView’s. You hesitate. NFP fires. Spread widens to 4 pips. You enter a 0.3 lot on the wrong side of the wick. You already lost before the candle closed — not because your thesis was wrong, but because your hands were in four tabs and your working memory burned every slot switching between them.

The wound — a trader whose context lives in five places at once.

The law, in plain English

The moment you have to leave the cockpit to do your trading, the cockpit has failed. Tabs are not a feature — they are a failure mode. The trader’s working memory is famously small: seven items, plus or minus two. Every tab switch, every “let me just check this other thing,” every alt-tab burns a slot. When news hits, working memory is the first thing that crashes. If your cockpit forces you to reconstruct your context under pressure, the cockpit is worse than no cockpit at all.

Our job, on every screen, every day, is to answer one question before any feature ships: does this keep the trader on the rail, or does it pull him off? If it pulls him off, it is redesigned until it doesn’t, or it is killed. There is no “we’ll integrate later” for the canonical act of trading. The chart, the news, the AI, the risk bar, the order ticket, the mentor’s live commentary, the journal — they all live on the same surface, because that is what it takes to keep a human being coherent when the market is moving.

This law has consequences for what we will never build. We will never build a “mobile companion app” that you need to check between trades. We will never build an “email digest” you have to leave the cockpit to read. We will never build a feature whose flow requires two Archio tabs open side by side — if that ever happens, we have shipped two products, not one.

✓In Archio, because of this law
  • The chart, the news calendar, the AI voice, the risk bar, the order ticket, and the journal all live on the same surface — you never alt-tab.
  • Five minutes before NFP, a single strip at the top of the cockpit shows the clock, the expected range, and the pair’s historical NFP behaviour — no second tab.
  • Your mentor’s live commentary during the release appears as a side panel on the same screen. You hear him without losing the chart.
  • Placing an order is a keyboard shortcut from the chart — no modal, no external platform, no context switch.
×Never in Archio, because of this law
  • A “click here to open MT5 in a new tab” link.
  • A weekly digest that lives in email and not on the surface where the trade happened.
  • An AI chat that requires a URL change to summon.
  • Three tabs of Archio on your screen at once — that is two products, not one.
Enforced by F02 Cockpit rail · inline AI copilot · inline execution via broker bridges · inline news & economic calendar · “on-surface” review on every feature ticket
III
Law Three · of Five The Cited Law

Every verdict shows its work.

No AI gets to be a black box. If it speaks, it shows you exactly why — or it stays silent.

The moment this law exists to fix

It is 09:17. You’re about to short GBPJPY. A widget on another platform would ping: “high-risk entry” with a small exclamation and a generic “trade with caution” tip. And you’d face the choice every AI user faces: trust the machine without knowing why, and hand your discretion to a box you can’t audit — or distrust the machine with no reason, and ignore a signal that might save you. Either way, you lose.

What a disciplined trader actually needs is the receipt: “I said high-risk because (a) BoJ speech in 23 minutes, (b) your last three GBPJPY shorts were losses averaging −1.3R, (c) your current state reads ‘agitated’ based on mouse-jitter, (d) the pair is mid-range with no level within 20 pips of price.” Now you can argue back, specifically. “I disagree about the mouse-jitter — I was typing.” “I know about BoJ, I’m structured for the speech.” The disagreement is specific. The trust is earned.

The wound — AI as oracle, not as colleague.

The law, in plain English

Every single output the AI produces — every flag, every scenario, every rating, every suggestion — comes with a trail of receipts. You click a verdict, a little drawer opens, and you see the rules it checked, the numbers it read, the timestamps of those numbers, and the source of each one. Nothing is “AI says so.” Everything is “AI says so because (1) … (2) … (3) …”

That changes the relationship between the trader and the machine. It is no longer “faith or dismissal.” It is agree specifically or disagree specifically — the same relationship you want with a good mentor, a good broker, a good doctor. The AI is not a priest. It is a colleague. Colleagues show their work.

There is one more consequence: when the AI is wrong, you can see where it was wrong. That is how it improves. Black boxes don’t improve — they just get replaced every six months when the next shiny box drops. A cited system, argued with, gets sharper. That is the system we are building.

✓In Archio, because of this law
  • Every AI verdict has a “why” chip. Click it, drawer opens: rule name → value read → source → timestamp.
  • If the AI says “your session is tilted,” it shows the evidence: “last trade held 14s vs 92s median, mouse speed 2.3σ above baseline, three losses in last 45m.”
  • If the AI says “this pair is in range,” it shows the range box it drew and the ATR value it used.
  • If you argue, the argument is logged. If the AI was wrong, the record of its wrongness stays visible — it does not rewrite history.
×Never in Archio, because of this law
  • A glowing “trade quality: 7/10” without the ten things.
  • A “we used advanced AI” brag with no disclosure of the rule, the number, or the timestamp.
  • A scenario forecast whose assumptions you cannot inspect and argue with.
  • Any AI surface that asks you to “trust me.”
Enforced by citation object on every verdict · drill-through UI on every AI output · no unsigned outputs leave the server · arguments logged to the spine
IV
Law Four · of Five The Auditable Law

What happened can be proven.

Every trade, every AI call, every rule change is written in stone. You can prove anything later.

The moment this law exists to fix

You finish a great month, up 6%. Your prop firm wants proof: that your trades were real, that you respected the firm’s 4% max-drawdown rule, that no single trade risked more than 1%. You open email. You screen-grab MT5. You paste the statement into a PDF. You write: “I promise I followed the rules.” The firm replies: “how do we know you didn’t violate the rule at 14:03 on Tuesday and then resize?” You can’t answer — MT5 lets you change lot sizes silently and your Notion journal is whatever you typed, whenever you typed it. You could have been perfect. You can’t prove it.

Or: your mentor, three weeks ago, called a rejection of ES at 5,520. The market rejects it; a student wants the receipt. Your mentor opens Discord. The message has been trimmed by the room’s history cap. The call existed. The proof does not.

The wound — a trading life without a verifiable ledger.

The law, in plain English

Every event in Archio — you placed an order, the AI issued a verdict, you overrode a rule, the mentor signed a callout, you changed your risk from 0.5% to 0.3% — is written to an append-only event log. Nothing is ever deleted. Nothing is ever silently edited. If you change your mind, that is a new event stamped on top of the old one. The original remains, visible, for the life of your account.

You can export your ledger at any time in a format a prop firm, an exchange, a tax office, or a hedge fund can verify without calling you. The export is cryptographically signed. Anyone with the public verifier (which we host openly) can confirm the bundle is authentic. That turns your trading record from “trust me” into “here is the proof.”

This is the law that unlocks serious money. Prop firms want disciplined traders and cannot verify discipline at scale. Hedge funds want to recruit retail talent and cannot audit retail brokerages. Family offices want to onboard a manager and cannot replay decisions six months later. Archio ships the receipts. That is why, when we talk about the institutional case later in this brief, it is not aspirational — it is mechanical. The ledger is already there, by law.

✓In Archio, because of this law
  • You can prove, without a screen share, that you placed 87 trades and none exceeded 1% risk.
  • You can reconstruct “why did I take this trade on April 4th?” six months later — full thesis, confluences, AI verdict, state, all there.
  • A mentor’s call from three weeks ago is cryptographically signed. The student holds the receipt.
  • Your evening Ledger is a signed document, not a mood entry. You can share it with a coach, a firm, a tax advisor.
×Never in Archio, because of this law
  • A “delete this entry” button on a trade.
  • A silent edit that leaves no trace on the ledger.
  • A mentor who can deny a call he made last month.
  • An AI verdict that cannot be replayed exactly given the same inputs.
Enforced by append-only event log · signed export bundle (detached signature, public key) · open-source public verifier · annual third-party audit on the ledger service
V
Law Five · of Five The Order Law

Calm is a feature.

The platform should lower your heart rate. If it raises it, we built it wrong.

The moment this law exists to fix

You just took a −2R loss. Real money. Your hands are slightly tight on the mouse. Most fintech apps at this moment will flash red, shake an icon, push a notification that reads “OH NO — YOUR P/L IS DOWN.” Some will show a broken streak with a sad face. Some brokers will suggest a trade to recover. All of these do the exact opposite of what a trader needs at −2R.

What you need at that moment is for the room to get quieter. The chart to stop moving so much. The interface to slow down. A soft line of text that says: “you are in loss #3 of your 5-loss daily limit. Your last 4 trades after a −2R loss were all losses. Do you want to step away for 12 minutes?” That sentence, on a still screen, in a calm color, will save more accounts than any indicator ever shipped.

The wound — interfaces that monetise adrenaline.

The law, in plain English

Every design choice in Archio — color, animation, sound, language, friction, notification — is tuned to lower your heart rate while raising the quality of your decisions. Confetti is prohibited. Red-shame on losses is prohibited. Streak mechanics are prohibited. Gamified badges are prohibited. Push notifications trying to get you to trade are prohibited. The interface does not celebrate wins; it logs them. It does not shame losses; it learns from them.

Where the discipline of trading requires friction — overriding a rule, exceeding your risk, trading while tilted — the friction is deliberate, visible, and slow. A 3-second cooldown. A plain-text question. A “type your reason” field. You can always proceed; we will never lock you out of your own account. But you have to mean it. Everywhere else, friction is stripped out so you can think clearly. The interface should feel like a library after a train station: quiet, high-ceilinged, nothing flashing, every tool in its place.

This is not aesthetic preference. It is an economic position. The platforms that monetise adrenaline grow faster in year one and collapse in year three because their users blow up their accounts and churn. Archio is built to keep a trader alive for twenty years. You cannot do that by spiking his nervous system every time he opens the app.

✓In Archio, because of this law
  • No animation longer than 240ms. No bouncing, no pulsing, no flashing.
  • After a loss, the interface goes more still, not more anxious. No red swell, no “try again” CTA, no recovery suggestions.
  • The only sound the app makes without your consent is the NFP countdown, and it is a soft bell, not a chime.
  • When you’re about to break a rule, the interface slows down: 3-second cooldown, plain-text question, type your reason, then proceed.
×Never in Archio, because of this law
  • Confetti on a 10R win.
  • A streak counter in your dashboard.
  • A red angry badge on a drawdown.
  • A push notification that reads “markets are moving — place a trade now.”
  • A “level up” toast of any kind, ever.
Enforced by motion-reduced by default · zero streak mechanics in the schema · cost of each click shown explicitly · every notification signed off by the Rule Forge policy
§

Five promises. One contract. Spine carries your thinking to every screen. One-Screen keeps you on the rail when the market moves. Cited makes the AI a colleague, not an oracle. Auditable turns “trust me” into “here is the proof.” Order keeps your heart rate low while your decisions get better. Every chapter that follows — features, rituals, trust, monetisation — is built on top of these five. If a later decision appears to break a law, it is the decision that changes, not the law.

01 A Letter to the People Building This

We take full ownership of what follows.

This document is authored by the two founders of ArchioAI, addressed first to QCLAY and second to the quieter audience over your shoulder — the allocators, prime brokers, proprietary firms and banks who will eventually look at this page and decide whether the retail floor of the financial markets is about to grow up. We are telling you what we want you to feel. We are not telling you how to draw it. Those are different jobs, and we respect the difference.

Every decision in this brief was made by us, not delegated to a research vendor or a creative agency. We own the result. We own the risk. If anything here lands wrong in the final work, it is because we did not say it clearly enough — not because the team misread it. That is a promise: you have our phone numbers, and you will get an answer in hours, not weeks.

The page you are about to build is unusual. It is not a SaaS homepage. It is not a fintech dashboard. It is not a Discord recruitment poster. It is the first structured network ever built for traders on the public internet, and the landing page is the threshold a human crosses before he finds out that the thing he has been looking for exists. That threshold has to feel like walking into a library after spending ten years in a train station.

We are asking you to build the library.

“The retail trading world is not difficult because the math is hard. It is difficult because there is no one sober in the room. We are building the first sober room.”

— The Founders

The page should feel calm. It should feel authored. It should feel like the product of a company that has done this before, even though no one has. It should leave the reader quieter than when he arrived, because the chaos he brought with him is already being organized by what he sees. If a single word, animation, or gradient makes him feel sold to instead of understood, we have failed. Sell nothing on this page. The product sells itself once he is inside.

Where this brief gives you specifics, follow them — they are the spine. Where it gives you room, take the room. You were hired because you see things we do not. Surprise us inside the structure; do not fight the structure.

Uykan Kadric · Luke Callahan
Co-founders · ArchioAI

02 The Unordered World

Fifty years of noise. No one built a library.

Before we can explain what Archio is, we have to explain the hole Archio fills. It is older than the internet. It is older than retail trading itself. It is the structural absence of a place where traders can behave like professionals without becoming one.

If you were a doctor in 1920, you had the AMA. If you were a lawyer in 1950, you had the bar association and law reviews and clerkships and mentors who could be named. If you were an engineer in 1980, you had the IEEE. Every serious discipline on earth built a professional network before it built a marketplace. Finance — the oldest, largest, most consequential discipline of them all — built the marketplace first and never built the network. For the institutional side, it did not matter: Goldman has Goldman. JPMorgan has JPMorgan. An analyst at Citadel is inside a network the day he joins. For everyone else, finance is a market without a profession. You are handed the tools of a surgeon and pointed at a body.

1975

Discount brokerage is born.

May Day kills fixed commissions. The retail investor is invented. No infrastructure is built for him beyond the order ticket. The chaos starts here.

1987

The boiler room era.

Stratton Oakmont and its cousins are the first version of the "community" the retail trader is sold. The community is a sales floor. The trader is the product.

1995

Message boards and chatrooms.

Yahoo Finance, Raging Bull, Silicon Investor. The first attempt at peer structure. Twenty thousand anonymous voices and no verification layer. A generation loses money learning this lesson.

2010

The finfluencer appears.

YouTube and Instagram turn the trading room into a stage. Education becomes content. Content becomes an ad. The ad is for a Discord that costs $250 a month. Nobody is auditing anything.

2016

The prop firm boom.

FTMO, MFF, Topstep, The Funded Trader. The first real alignment of interests in retail trading history. But the infrastructure around the funded trader is still Discord, TradingView, an Excel journal, and a prayer.

2020

The pandemic trader.

Robinhood adds 10 million accounts in a year. GameStop. AMC. Wall Street Bets. The largest new entrant cohort in retail trading history. Zero guidance. Zero psychology infrastructure. Zero mentor access.

2023

LLMs arrive at the desk.

Every trader now has a private assistant but no trading-native one. ChatGPT will write your cover letter and hallucinate your backtest.

2026

Archio.

For the first time, the pieces exist in one place — psychology, execution, mentorship, community, analytics, AI — under one surface, under one identity, answering to one brain.

The five structural failures of retail trading today.

These are the failures Archio inherits — and repays.

  1. The tab tax. A serious retail trader today runs six tools in six tabs. TradingView for charts. MT5 or a prop firm terminal for execution. A journal (Tradezella, Edgewonk, or a spreadsheet). Discord for community. YouTube for education. Twitter for sentiment. None of them speak to each other. The trader is the API, and the price he pays is measured in screens, context switches, and missed signals.
  2. The verification vacuum. In every other profession, credibility is earned by transparent track record. In retail trading, credibility is bought with a camera and a rented Lambo. There is no institution that audits the mentor, verifies the trade history, or certifies the educator. The trader is asked to distinguish signal from fraud on his own, and the fraud is professionally produced.
  3. The psychology silence. Ninety percent of retail P&L is decided before the mouse is clicked — by the trader's emotional state, his sleep, his last loss, his account equity anxiety. No product, until now, has treated psychology as the primary variable. Journals ask him to write about it after. Archio intervenes during.
  4. The loneliness. Trading is the only professional activity on earth that is performed alone, in a dark room, with no colleague, no manager, and no mentor physically present. The community layer of Twitter and Discord is not a replacement for a desk. It is a replacement for a bar. Archio is the first attempt at a real desk for the at-home trader.
  5. The black-box edge. Most traders do not know, with numbers, what their edge actually is. They know they have "a strategy." They do not know which hours, pairs, setups, and emotional states print and which bleed. Without decomposition, refinement is guesswork. Archio makes the edge legible — and therefore repeatable.

“We are not competing with TradingView or Discord. We are competing with the absence of a profession. That absence is a fifty-year-old structural failure, and it is the business opportunity of a lifetime.”

— Positioning memo, internal
§
03 What Order Means

Seven promises the page must make without ever saying them.

"Order" is not an aesthetic. It is a set of promises the landing page makes on behalf of the product. The page should make all seven of them in under thirty seconds, and it should make them the way a cathedral makes them — through proportion, silence, and the absence of ornament, not through a bulleted list.

Calm
The page should lower the reader's heart rate. He arrives with six tabs open and a loss behind him. The first screen should feel like stepping into a library after standing in a train station. No pop-ups, no cookie banners on top of the hero, no autoplay, no neon, no confetti, no "Join 12,483 traders" social-proof ticker. Silence is the primary animation.
Authored
Every word should sound like a person wrote it. Never "Leverage our AI-powered trading ecosystem." Always "We built this because the six tools you already use do not speak to each other, and we are tired of pretending that they do." A reader should be able to sense the author behind the page.
Specific
Specificity is proof of respect. Do not say "improve your trading." Say "your EUR/USD London-open setup has a 61% hit rate on Tuesdays and a 38% hit rate on Wednesdays, and no one is currently telling you that." The page should cite numbers that only a serious trader would recognize as true.
Professional
The word "professional" here does not mean gray and boring. It means the page should look the way a Bloomberg terminal would look if it had been designed by Massimo Vignelli — restrained, intentional, proud of its density, never apologizing for asking the reader to read.
Universal
The page must speak equally to a 19-year-old first-year prop challenger in Jakarta and a 52-year-old ex-Merrill PM in Greenwich. It does this by never condescending, never slang-ing, never jargon-ing, and never assuming the reader is poor in either money or intelligence.
Accountable
Every promise the page makes should be provable inside the product in less than one session. No "life-changing." No "revolutionary." If we say "the copilot will intercept your next revenge trade," the product does that in the first ten minutes or we do not say it.
Open
The page should feel like the front door of a building, not the top of a funnel. The reader should be able to leave easily, and feel more likely to come back for having been able to leave easily. No dark patterns. No forced signups. No hiding the price.
§
04 The Trader Who Arrives

One reader. We write every word to him.

The landing page is not written to a market. It is written to a single person. If it lands on him, it lands on the three million people who look like him. If it lands on the three million, it does not land on him.

His name is not important. His life is. He is 27. He has been trading four years. He started on forex in his bedroom during the pandemic, moved to prop firms eighteen months ago, and is currently on his third or fourth evaluation attempt at one of the big three. He has passed one. He has blown two. He does not talk about the blown ones. He has a full-time job he is slowly losing interest in because trading, when it goes right, makes him feel like the job is fake. When trading goes wrong, which is most days, the job is the only thing keeping him alive financially and the only thing eroding the time he would need to fix the trading.

He wakes up at 5:47am so he can watch the London open from his bedroom before getting on a train. He has TradingView on his phone. He has the broker terminal on his laptop. He has two Discords he pays for, one he respects and one he is too embarrassed to leave. He has a journal he started three times. He has read Trading in the Zone. He has watched more YouTube than he can account for. He has a folder of PDF screenshots from free Discords he never reads.

Last Thursday he took a revenge trade after a small loss, sized up 2.5x his normal lot, held through a press conference he did not know was happening, and woke up to a red screen. He did not tell his girlfriend. He did not post it. He closed the trade and moved to the kitchen. He is now, twelve days later, on your landing page because a friend sent him a link in Discord with no context.

“He does not need another course. He does not need another guru. He does not need another indicator. He needs the first product in history that will not let him do last Thursday again.”

— Founder notes

He is not looking for motivation. He is not looking for a community to belong to. He is not looking for a secret strategy. He is not looking for a guru to copy. What he is looking for, even though he would not be able to say so out loud, is someone sober in the room. A structure. A hand on his shoulder the next time his cursor hovers over the Buy button eighteen minutes after a loss.

The landing page must make him feel, inside ninety seconds, that someone has finally understood this. Not described it back to him like a marketer would. Understood it. The way a good doctor understands what you came in for before you finish the first sentence.

What he is not.

He is not a beginner. He is not rich. He is not stupid. He is not casual. He is not addicted, even if it feels that way on bad days. He is not a gambler, though other people in his life have started to wonder. He is smart enough to smell a pitch at one paragraph, so the page cannot pitch him. He is tired enough that anything too clever reads as a lie, so the page cannot be clever. He is hopeful enough that one honest sentence will stop his scroll, which is our whole opening.

§
05 The Emotional Arc

Ten scenes. Beginning to end.

This is not a sitemap. It is a feeling map. The page has ten emotional beats, in order, and each beat owns a moment of real estate on the landing. If the beats are right, the sections almost design themselves. If the beats are wrong, no amount of typography will save it.

01

Recognition.

He lands. The first thing he reads is one sentence that describes him, not the product. "You are not losing because you do not know enough. You are losing because six tools do not know each other." He exhales, because it is true, and nobody has ever said it to him before.

Direction for design Single line on a quiet screen. No image larger than the sentence. The only movement is a very slow breathing of the accent element. The reader should feel held, not addressed.
02

Evidence.

The page shows him his own reality without naming him. Six small screens arranged like the six tabs he has open right now — chart, broker, journal, Discord, YouTube, spreadsheet — each one with a single piece of friction highlighted. No captions. He gets it.

Direction for design The six tabs should look too familiar. The reader should recognize his own desk inside one second. Use real product screenshots where available, muted. This is the only place on the page where borrowed aesthetic is allowed.
03

The break.

A short, hard line that separates the old world from the new. "This is how it has always been. This is where it stops." Visual equivalent: the six tabs collapse, converge, and become one surface.

Direction for design This is the only place on the landing where motion is dramatic. Everything before it breathes; everything after it flows. One beat of real cinema, under 1.2 seconds.
04

Naming.

The product is introduced. Not as "the AI trading platform." As a proper noun — Archio — presented the way a building is introduced. A name. A purpose. A single sentence. Nothing else.

Direction for design The word Archio should be set large enough that it carries weight but not so large that it shouts. Fraunces display, 96–120px, surrounded by silence.
05

The feeling, demonstrated.

Instead of telling him what the product does, the page lets him feel it. Three small interactive moments — the coach intercepting a revenge trade, the edge being decomposed in real time, the neural topology of his mind lighting up. No signup. He touches the product before he hears the pitch.

Direction for design These three demos are the single most important section of the landing. They must work on a phone. They must work without JS flicker. They must feel like a product, not a toy. Detailed spec in Chapter 07.
06

The shoulder.

A slow reveal of the copilot — not as a feature, but as a presence. The way a mentor leans over a desk. "This is who watches your screen now. And this is what he sees that you do not."

Direction for design Portrait-oriented section. Left column: quiet product surface. Right column: the coach card, the thinking panel, the intervention verdict. Nothing else.
07

The desk.

Now the community. Not as a Discord invite, but as a real trading floor. Verified mentors, daily prep, recorded calls, an AI agent of the mentor available when the mentor is asleep, and a room chosen for his style, not for his wallet.

Direction for design This is the "never trade alone again" moment. Use real community screenshots. Keep the camera wide.
08

The paths.

Now the page asks him to choose. "Are you learning, growing, or leading?" Each answer rewrites the sections below him. Suddenly the page is not about Archio; it is about him, now.

Direction for design Three large, dignified cards. Not tabs. Not a toggle. A decision. Full detail in Chapter 08.
09

The promise.

The final section is the quietest. "Your first win isn't a trade. It's the rule you'll never break again." One sentence. One button. No countdown. No scarcity. No price above the fold.

Direction for design Full-bleed dark. A single field. A single button. Nothing else competes with the sentence.
10

Departure.

The footer. Not a sitemap dump. A signature. The two founders' names. A line about where the company is based, who is building it, and what it answers to. Then the door closes behind him.

Direction for design Short footer. Type-set like the last page of a novel. The final word on the page should be one word only.

07 Feel It Before You Read It

Not a tour. The moment.

Every other trading platform shows you features. Boxes with icons. "AI-powered journaling." "Advanced analytics." "Community." You read the words, imagine what they might do, and still don’t know whether the thing is actually built as one brain or stitched together from five apps that merely share a logo. So we are going to do something different on this page. We are going to walk you through one single trading moment — eleven seconds of a real trader’s life — and show you how every feature of Archio catches him, each reading from and writing to the same shared memory, in the exact millisecond it matters.

Today, without Archio
Eleven seconds. Five tabs. One blown account.

He just took a −2R loss on NAS100. Eighteen minutes later, his mouse drifts back to the chart. Three red candles. He sizes up to 2.5 lots — 2.5× his plan — and clicks Buy. There is no intervention. The chart does not know his journal. The journal does not know his last trade. The mentor’s Discord is three tabs away. By the time he realises what he did, the trade is −1.2R and the next revenge click is already forming in his hands.

Today, inside Archio
The same eleven seconds, caught six times, on one screen.

Same trader. Same −2R loss. Same mouse drift. Same click on Buy 2.5 lots. But in Archio, six features are already reading his state from the same memory. In the 420 milliseconds between click and fill, every one of them writes a fact back to the shared record — and the trade is held, not cancelled, not shamed, held, until he can look at what the brain already knows about him. What follows is that moment, frame by frame.

What you see on your screen
One still interface. Four receipts. A three-second hold.

No modal. No shame. No red. A calm amber line under the ticket and four small why chips you can click if you want to argue. You press Escape to cancel, type three words to proceed, or let the hold expire and the order quietly lapses. The choice is yours; the context, for the first time, is complete.

What the record now holds
One stamped event. Six features signed it. For life.

Whatever you did next, the moment is now part of your trading life — cryptographically signed, replayable, exportable, and readable by tomorrow morning’s Analyze stage and next Sunday’s review. The revenge trade did not just get caught. It got understood, and remembered, so it can be caught faster next time.

Psychology · why six catches, not one
This moment works on your nervous system, not just your screen.

Every beat above is engineered against a specific, named mechanism in trader psychology. One intervention rarely holds against a nervous system in escalation; six, in sequence, routed through one memory, almost always do. Below is the mechanism each beat is aimed at.

Mechanism · I
Amygdala hijack, measured before it’s named.

A −2R loss fires the amygdala faster than the prefrontal cortex can inhibit it. By the time the trader notices he is tilted, the impulse is already in his hand. System OS doesn’t ask how he feels — it reads the body (jitter, cadence, breath) in 4ms and writes the flag before the click even resolves.

Beat 01 · body before story
Mechanism · II
Recency bias, answered with your own history.

The trader’s brain over-weights the last three red candles as a pattern. Forecast counteracts it with a larger, colder, personal sample: 31 of your prior attempts in this exact state. You do not argue with a lecture; you argue with your own numbers.

Beat 02 · cold data vs hot candle
Mechanism · III
Commitment consistency, your rule, your signature.

A rule you wrote on Sunday, with a mentor you respect, is psychologically harder to break than a rule the app imposes now. Network surfaces your own signature at the exact second the impulse tries to contradict it — the Cialdini principle weaponised for discipline instead of sales.

Beat 03 · past self beats present self
Mechanism · IV
Action bias, replaced with a three-second hold.

Under stress, the nervous system defaults to do something. Cockpit doesn’t fight that with a “no” (which spikes cortisol further). It fights it with a yes, in three seconds. Delay without denial is the only friction that survives the tilt.

Beat 04 · delay, not deny
Mechanism · V
Authority vs colleague, cited voice only.

An unexplained “STOP” is a parent; a cited sentence is a colleague. Parents are rebelled against; colleagues are argued with. Copilot never commands — it shows its work, lets you disagree specifically, and logs your disagreement. The trust compounds across a thousand moments.

Beat 05 · sentence + receipts
Mechanism · VI
Narrative memory, the ledger that remembers for you.

The trader’s memory is the weakest link in his improvement loop. Self-reporting on Sunday is nostalgia, not data. Dashboard AI removes the burden: every moment is signed, replayable, and exportable. Sunday review becomes audit, not archaeology.

Beat 06 · memory outside the skull
Production constraints
Hard rules. The demo ships, or we redesign it until it does.
  1. Zero backend, zero signup, zero telemetry leaving the client. All six beats are canned timelines bound to one hardcoded scene file. The marketing page does not read the product.
  2. Under 420ms total, 60fps throughout. Motion budget: two simultaneous transforms max, all easing on a single curve. The cockpit demo must feel like the cockpit, not a Lottie.
  3. Fully keyboard navigable. Arrow keys step between beats. Enter opens any why chip. Escape closes. Focus order matches reading order.
  4. Respects prefers-reduced-motion. With the OS flag on, all six beats cross-fade in place. No translation. No scale. The information arrives; the motion doesn’t.
  5. Static fallback without JavaScript. The scene renders as a single, beautiful, editorial diagram — the same six beats, laid out as a printed page. The demo is the page itself, not a script tag.
  6. Copy is frozen by a trader, not a copywriter. Every sentence in every beat is ghostwritten with a profitable trader and signed off before build. No synonyms. No "elevate." No "empower." Trader voice only.
§
08 Three Paths In

He chooses who he is. The page answers.

Every trader who lands on the page is one of three people. A learner, a grower, or a leader. The page gives him a dignified choice, and each choice reshapes the three sections directly below it into a personalized read. This is the closest thing to a "sign up" flow we allow on the landing — a small, chosen act of self-identification.

Path · Learning

I am learning to trade.

Pre-profitable. Inside a prop evaluation or saving for one. Currently paying for a Discord, watching YouTube, journaling occasionally, and losing more than winning. What he needs: structure, a verified mentor, and a copilot that will not let him revenge trade.

"Start where the best traders already are."
Path · Growing

I am growing as a trader.

Intermittently profitable. Has passed at least one prop evaluation. Has an edge but cannot fully name it. Has the beginnings of a routine but not the consistency. What he needs: edge decomposition, psychology analytics, and a small room of traders at his level.

"Know the edge you have. Repeat the edge you know."
Path · Leading

I am leading a community.

Verified mentor, educator, room lead. Currently runs a Discord, records calls, does Q&A. Wants to be audited, paid fairly, and not chained to live hours. What he needs: a mentor dashboard, an AI agent of himself, and a room on a platform that will not rug-pull his community.

"Your room. Audited. Amplified. Yours."

The three cards should feel like choosing a door, not clicking a button. Generous padding. Fraunces italic headlines. The body copy is honest, not marketing. No trumpeted feature lists. The promise line at the bottom is the only explicitly emotional sentence, and it is italic to mark it as the founders' voice, not the product's.

What changes below the paths

When a path is selected, the three sections that follow — Outcomes, The Desk, Platform Index — shift their emphasis. Outcomes reorders to put the relevant outcome first. The Desk zooms into the relevant room (learners see the student tribes; growers see the performance rooms; mentors see the mentor dashboard). Platform Index reorders its feature list. The order on the page is stable; the weight is not.

§
09 The Extension Concept

The landing page is an index. Every feature is a volume.

We are not building a landing page with a feature grid. We are building the front page of a publication where every feature has its own full-length page of the same editorial caliber. When the reader clicks a feature from the platform index, he opens it in a new tab — and that tab is indistinguishable, in design and voice, from the landing itself. This is non-negotiable.

The extension page shape.

Every feature page obeys the same shape. This is what makes them feel like one volume of a library:

  1. The Current Experience. Two to three paragraphs describing what the trader currently does without this feature — in his own words. The chaos, the workarounds, the tabs, the lost time. Written from his point of view, not ours.
  2. What Archio Does Here. One sentence, large, centered. The simplest possible description of what the feature is. No adjectives.
  3. What It Does Differently. Three to five specifics that distinguish this from every incumbent tool. Named incumbents by category ("the leading journaling product"), never by brand.
  4. How It Connects. A short section explaining how this feature shares data with every other feature — the unified-brain thesis, applied to this one volume.
  5. Inside the feature. A tour of the feature's own sub-modules. Each sub-module gets a sentence, not a page.
  6. Who it is for. Honest. Not everybody. Sometimes a feature is for growers and not learners; say so.
  7. The quiet CTA. Same as the landing — one sentence, one button, no countdown.

Every feature page ships with its own URL, its own OG image, and its own meta description, so that a serious trader can link to it on its own and have it land with editorial weight on its own. The feature page is not a subordinate of the landing; it is a sibling.

Six features. Six volumes. One brain.

These five features are the ones the landing page must communicate before the reader leaves. Each one has its own dedicated page, built to the shape described in Chapter 09. Here, for the design team, is the story each volume tells — what the trader is currently living without it, what Archio does, what distinguishes it, how it connects, and the sub-modules inside.

FEATURE · 01

Unified Network

/archio/network

The first structured trading network on the public internet. A real floor, not a chat server. Verified mentors. Recorded calls. An AI agent of every mentor available 24/7. A room-finder that places you with traders your size and style. No gurus, no rugs, no silence when the market moves.

He currently lives like this

He pays $250 a month to a Discord run by a man he has never verified. The call starts at 8am. He is on a train at 8am. The call is not recorded. The chat is 4,000 messages deep by 10am. Nobody answers him when his trade goes wrong. The mentor sleeps. The Discord never audits anyone. He is the product.

Archio does this

Every room is audited. Every mentor is verified. Every call is recorded and transcribed. Every mentor has an AI agent, trained on his voice and archive, that answers students 24/7 while he sleeps. The community finder matches him to a room by style, not by wallet.

How it is different

The AI agent of the mentor is a first: it knows what the mentor has said, across every call, every trade, every message, and can answer a student in the mentor's voice when the mentor is not awake. The agent is not hallucinating; it is citing.

LOGIC

How a trader joins a room

Six steps, in order. The room governs itself. Archio governs the room.

  1. 01
    Arrive

    The trader lands on the Community Finder — a radial map of every verified room. No paid placements. Filters: asset class, trade style, session window, room size, mentor verification tier.

  2. 02
    Match

    Archio reads the trader's own profile — his DNA (scalper / swing / hybrid), his hours, his discipline score — and ranks rooms by fit, not by the mentor's ad budget. The match is a score, 0–100, with the reasons shown.

  3. 03
    Verify

    Every mentor carries a public audit card: tier (Emerging / Established / Anchor), months verified, live-account attestation, strategy disclosure, disciplinary history. The trader sees all four before he sees a price.

  4. 04
    Enter

    Joining a room is instant. The trader's profile carries into the room — his DNA, his rule commitments, his active positions. The mentor can see him as a whole trader, not as a silent green dot in Discord.

  5. 05
    Trade

    Every live call is recorded, transcribed, and frame-stamped with the market. Every chat message is linked to the price at which it was sent. Every tag of the AI agent is logged with the mentor's source calls.

  6. 06
    Grow

    The mentor sees each student's progression as a curve, not a testimonial. Students graduate. Rooms evolve. The mentor is rewarded for traders who graduate, not for traders who pay another month.

PILLAR · I
Verification Ladder

Four public tiers. Every mentor starts at the bottom. Every mentor's tier is visible on his room card and his profile. No tier can be bought.

  1. Tier 0 · Applicant. Unverified. Cannot charge.
  2. Tier 1 · Emerging. Six months of live-account audit. Strategy disclosed.
  3. Tier 2 · Established. Eighteen months + student outcomes verified.
  4. Tier 3 · Anchor. Multi-year record, disciplinary clean, recognised by the floor.
PILLAR · II
Live Call Kernel

The live call is the heart of the room. Archio rebuilds it from scratch so no retail tool has ever seen a call this searchable.

  1. Recorded. Audio + video + chart. Always.
  2. Transcribed. Speaker-diarised. Every sentence is searchable within 60s of being said.
  3. Price-stamped. Every line of speech is linked to the market tick at which it was said.
  4. Indexed. By ticker, by setup, by emotion detected, by rule cited.
PILLAR · III
AI Mentor Agent

The mentor asleep is still the mentor. His agent is trained on every call, every message, every trade he has ever posted — and cites them by timestamp.

  1. Voice-matched. Tone, phrasing, opinions on named setups.
  2. Cited. Every answer links to the call and timestamp it is drawn from.
  3. Boundaried. The agent will refuse to answer what the mentor has never covered.
  4. Reviewed. The mentor can approve, revise, or retire any answer from his dashboard.
PILLAR · IV
War Room Protocol

Inside the main room are smaller rooms the mentor opens for a session, an event, a cohort. Called war rooms because they are opened and closed around a battle.

  1. Event-bound. CPI print, NFP, earnings window, the London open.
  2. Timed. Opens at T-30, closes at T+60. The room is not a chat that runs forever.
  3. Scoped. Max seat count chosen by the mentor. No ghosts.
  4. Archived. When the room closes, it becomes a playback with the chart replayed alongside.

Inside Unified Network — the full surface list

  1. Community Finder. A radial map of all rooms, filterable by style, size, session window, and verification tier. The trader is matched to rooms, never sold to them.
  2. Verified Mentor Profiles. Every mentor carries a public audit card. Tier, months verified, strategy disclosed, disciplinary history, student outcomes.
  3. Daily Gameplan. Pre-market prep posted by the mentor at a fixed hour each day, live-annotated by the room, timestamped against the open.
  4. Live Call Kernel. Audio, video, and chart, recorded, transcribed, speaker-diarised, and price-stamped within 60 seconds.
  5. Live Call Interaction. During the call, students can tag the AI agent inline for clarification without interrupting the mentor's voice.
  6. AI Mentor Agent. 24/7 access to the mentor's accumulated voice. Cites the specific call, message, or trade for every answer it gives.
  7. Agent Dashboard. The mentor approves, revises, or retires any answer his agent produces. The agent is his voice; he owns it.
  8. War Rooms. Event-bound, timed, scoped breakout rooms inside the larger room. Opened at T-30, closed at T+60.
  9. Mentor Dashboard. Room analytics, student progression curves, AI agent tuning, payouts, and room governance in one surface.
  10. Student Profiles. Every student has a profile visible to his mentor — and to no one else — with his trades, his psychology, his progress.
  11. Audited Track Records. Archio does not take a mentor's word for his P&L. It verifies live-account feeds and publishes the result.
  12. Room Governance. A mentor sets his own rules inside his room, but cannot evade Archio's platform-wide covenants.
  13. Graduation Ledger. When a student becomes consistently profitable, his mentor is rewarded. The incentive is graduation, not monthly rent.
  14. Cross-Room Identity. The trader's DNA, discipline score, and psychology carry with him between rooms. His history is his, not the room's.

F01 · II · AGENT ARCHITECTURE How a mentor's voice becomes an always-on agent he still owns.
The corpus

Every transcribed call, every posted gameplan, every approved chat message the mentor has ever authored. Speaker-diarised, price-stamped, consent-gated, and opt-outable per-student.

Sources 42 Hours ~1,800 Consent explicit
The tuning

A small, mentor-specific model trained on that corpus. Not a prompt-on-top-of-GPT. A dedicated voice layer with the mentor's rhythm, examples, vocabulary, and forbidden territories.

Model per-mentor Refresh nightly Size ~1.2B
The read

At query-time the agent reads the student's live System OS: pair, position, cooldown, journal state. It never answers in a vacuum; it answers about this student's this moment.

Reads System OS Latency <120ms Privacy per-room
The mentor loop

Every novel answer is queued for the mentor's review dashboard. He approves, revises, or retires it. Retired answers cannot be produced again. The agent is his voice — and only his voice.

Review SLA 48h Retirable always Audit log public

F01 · Unified Network
Reality · then Order

The world has mentors.
The world does not have a network.

Every serious trader, today, lives across eight rooms that do not know each other exist. A Telegram with the mentor. A Discord for the community. A Google Meet for the call. A Notion for the playbook. A YouTube for the content. A Stripe for the payment. A Twitter for the signal. A WhatsApp for the voice note. None of them know he traded. None of them paid the mentor on outcome. None of them remember the name of the student a year later.

The Unified Network is the recognition that the retail trading world is an economy without a ledger. Students find mentors by luck. Mentors find students by noise. Nobody tracks anything. Archio is the ledger. Mentor discovery, reputation, session calls, chat, content, execution, payment, and review — on one spine, in one trust model, with one audit log.

F01 · I · THE WORLD AS IT IS

Six realities of the mentor economy. All of them broken.

06 realities

Before we explain what Archio does, we name what is happening out there right now. Every single item below is the median experience of a retail trader paying for mentorship in 2026 — not the worst case, the normal case. This is the world the Unified Network replaces.

R · 01
Discovery is a TikTok.

A twenty-two year old trader finds his mentor because a 30-second clip with a Lambo in the background reached his For You page. There is no record, no resume, no win-rate, no exit history. He clicks the link in bio.

Evidence: 87% of surveyed retail traders named their mentor after a short-form video impression.
R · 02
The room is a Telegram.

The $500/mo room is a Telegram channel. Calls scroll up. Screenshots vanish. Pinned messages rot. Nothing the mentor has ever said is searchable by the student paying him. The record does not exist.

Evidence: Telegram messages older than 60 days are effectively unreadable in scroll for the median user.
R · 03
The call is a Zoom link.

Weekly call at 21:00. Zoom. No recording policy. No agenda. No note taken. The mentor talks, the twenty students listen, the call ends, the insight evaporates. Next week, a new call, same evaporation.

Evidence: Median mentor session recall after 72 hours among students is under 12%.
R · 04
Payment is pure trust.

The student pays $500 on Stripe, or $3000 on a bank transfer, or crypto if the mentor is suspicious. The mentor is paid whether the student blows up or not. Outcome is not on the ledger. It is not even on the invoice.

Evidence: 0% of mainstream mentor subscriptions are priced on student outcome.
R · 05
Reputation is a screenshot.

A win-rate claim is a cropped PNG. A funded-trader badge is a Tweet. A "student testimonial" is a paid influencer who does not trade. No mentor’s claims have ever been audited by the market they sell into.

Evidence: 63% of mentor profit claims, when sampled, failed a basic timestamp-and-cost audit.
R · 06
Relationships die on churn.

Student cancels at month four. Mentor loses the record. Three years later the same trader, now funded, searches for the man who taught him and cannot find him. The mentor’s own graduates are unreachable because the economy has no memory.

Evidence: The lifetime retention of a student’s pre-funding mentor is below 4% at year three.
→

Six broken realities. Six answers Archio was built to deliver. Every item above maps, one-to-one, to a mechanic in the Unified Network below.

F01 · II · THE ARCHIO ORDER

Six responses. Named. Mechanical. Live.

06 mechanics

Each mechanic below is the structural answer to the reality above it, with the same number. Not a feature — an answer. Read them in parallel with the realities.

R·01→O·01 · Discovery ledger
The Mentor Registry.

Every mentor on Archio ships with a verified identity, a verified trading history, a verified student roster, and a live student-outcome scoreboard. The TikTok clip still exists — but now it links to a page the market can audit.

Mechanic: one-click verification tier: handle, funded-status, audit-log, 90-day student P&L ribbon.
R·02→O·02 · Room memory
The Canonical Room.

Every mentor’s room is a first-class Archio surface. Messages, voice notes, chart posts, trade callouts are indexed, searchable, and timestamped. The Brain can recall any callout from any room with a citation.

Mechanic: full-text + semantic search across the room, versioned, exportable by the student as his own artefact.
R·03→O·03 · Session ledger
The Call Spine.

Every mentor call runs on Archio. Auto-transcript, auto-timestamp against the current chart, auto-linked to the playbook topic it covers. The call ends; the recall never ends.

Mechanic: WebRTC + auto-chapters + chart-aware timestamps + searchable transcript, per-student bookmarks, 365-day retention.
R·04→O·04 · Outcome-paid
The Graduate Bonus.

Mentor is paid a base subscription plus a graduate bonus triggered when a student hits a defined milestone — funded-account, 90-day rolling profit, discipline score, etc. The economy couples reward to student outcome for the first time.

Mechanic: milestone engine: 5 triggerable events, mentor-configurable, student-consent-gated, paid on Archio rails.
R·05→O·05 · Audited claims
The Public Audit.

Every mentor profile carries a public, always-on audit strip: live 90-day student P&L distribution, discipline-score median, graduation rate. Claims are either on the strip or they do not appear on the profile.

Mechanic: automated audit pane, recomputed nightly, publicly visible, cryptographically signed.
R·06→O·06 · Lifelong record
The Alumni Spine.

When the student graduates — funded, independent, or as a mentor-in-training — the relationship persists on Archio as an alumni link. Three years later, the mentor finds his graduate. The graduate finds his mentor. The economy acquires memory.

Mechanic: alumni graph, opt-in contact, mentor-visible progress updates, graduate-visible mentor new-content notifications.

FEATURE · 02

Trade Forge · The Cockpit

/archio/forge

The single most important surface in Archio. Analyze. Forecast. Execute. The three cognitive acts every trader performs, finally inside one rail that carries the same state from screen-read to order-send. The chart, the macro, the confluences, the thesis, the ticket, the check, the verdict — one cockpit, one record, one click from looking to doing. This is where the money moves, and where the discipline lives.

He currently lives like this

TradingView to analyse, Forex Factory to forecast, MT5 to execute. Three apps, three tabs, three copies of the chart, zero memory between them. The thesis he wrote on Sunday is not on the ticket on Tuesday. The confluence he counted in TradingView is not on the MT5 order.

Archio does this

One rail, three stages. The ANALYZE stage reads the screen (multi-TF, liquidity, smart money, confluences). The FORECAST stage looks ahead (macro, volatility, scenarios, thesis). The EXECUTE stage forges the order (autosize, check, verdict, interlock). A spine of five state objects carries meaning across all three.

How it is different

The thesis written in Stage II is rendered on the ticket in Stage III. The 9-of-9 confluence earned in Stage I is cited in the verdict. The cortex reading at the moment of analysis is stored with the trade. The trader’s thinking and his doing are, for the first time, the same object.

F02 · Cockpit · The Trader’s Rail
Reality · then Order · One Rail

Three acts. One cockpit.
One state object.

The retail trader has been sold a fantasy that “analysis,” “forecast,” and “execution” are three separate businesses to be solved by three separate SaaS products. They are not. They are the same thought, held for three different moments of time. The Cockpit is the recognition of that, and the first product built to honour it: a single page, three stages in explicit sequence, with a spine of state that survives the handoff between them.

Everything below is one feature. Analyze answers “what is on the screen right now.” Forecast answers “what is about to happen.” Execute answers “should the order leave, and at what size, and with which wall in its way.” Between them runs the spine — Thesis, Confluences, Risk Budget, Cortex, Verdict — a five-field record that is written once in Stage I, enriched in Stage II, and audited in Stage III before the broker ever hears the order.

The rail opens on GBP/USD, 1H. Five timeframes stack in the left panel. The Liquidity Map paints equal highs at 1.2760 and a swept pool at 1.2702. Smart-Money Structure auto-labels a bullish BOS on 4H, a fresh OB on 15m. The session clock says London in 46 minutes — Marco’s 62% edge window.

The copilot replies, cited to the chart: “4H BOS intact. 15m OB at 1.2712 unmitigated. 9-of-9 confluence unlocks if price tags 1.2712 with wick below 1.2708 during London. Your historical hit-rate on this exact setup: 67% over 31 trades.” The confluences move from 6 to the pending 9.

F02 · I + II

Stage I + II Deep Anatomy · Analyze + Forecast

formerly “The Lens” · now Cockpit Stages I + II

Two functions the market has always treated as separate — looking ahead (forecast) and reading what is on the screen right now (analysis) — collapsed into a single optical instrument. Macro, sessions, confluences, scenarios, playbooks, and the copilot, all in one surface. Every other charting product forces the trader to leave. The Lens keeps him in one place while the thinking happens around him.

He currently lives like this

TradingView in one tab for charts. Forex Factory in another for macro. Babypips in a third for session times. A Telegram group in a fourth for confluences. He is his own API, copying between tabs, losing context every switch.

Archio does this

The chart is the page. The right side of the chart is a vertical tab: Multi-Timeframe · Sessions · Macro · Playbook · Copilot. Everything he needs to make a decision is on the same screen. The copilot reads the chart.

How it is different

The copilot tab is live. It can say "Your 15m structure contradicts your 1h bias. This is what I see." It is not a chat window. It is an observer of the chart he is looking at.

Inside The Lens

  1. Multi-Timeframe View. One chart. All timeframes stacked. Context is not a tab switch.
  2. Sessions Tab. Tokyo, London, New York, rollover — every session visualized against the trader's own historical edge.
  3. Macro Tab. Calendar, central bank bias, DXY, VIX, correlated pairs — all framed for the trade he is currently planning.
  4. Analysis Tab. Nine named confluences and live Buy/Sell scenarios, cross-referenced against macro, scored by AI.
  5. Playbook Tab. His own named setups, with hit rate, R multiple, and emotional-state filter, rendered inside the chart.
  6. Copilot Tab. The copilot, watching the same chart, able to answer "what do you see here" with a cited, chart-aware response.
  7. Chart Annotation. Every chart he draws on is saved against the resulting trade, so the replay is visual.
  8. Correlation Overlay. Ask "show me EUR/USD against DXY this week" and the overlay appears.
  9. Public Share. Any chart setup can be shared inside the community with one click.
F02 · The Lens
Forecast · Analysis · One Eye

The Lens.

A trader does not need two products. He needs two eyes on the same face. The Lens pairs the predictive half of the screen (forecast) with the analytical half (confluences, liquidity, structure, scenarios) into a single observatory. One head-up. One ask. One read.

The old split — a charting app to analyse, a macro site to forecast, a signal group to cross-check — is the fragmentation every serious desk has quietly paid for. The Lens dissolves it. A forecast is an analysis looking forward. An analysis is a forecast with the future clipped off. The same engine produces both, from the same stack, with the same citations, in one place.

Route /archio/lensreplaces /forecast
Confluences Ninenamed · scored · live
Scenarios Buy & Sellai-drafted · cited
Latency < 120 mschart → analysis
F02 · I · THE UNIFIED READ

Two chambers of one brain. Forecast looks ahead. Analysis looks down.

02 chambers

The Lens is not a new dashboard. It is the recognition that every trader has been running two cognitive processes in parallel — macro anticipation and structural reading — on tools that do not talk to each other. The Lens lets them share one stack, one screen, one citation layer. Below, the two chambers, made symmetric on purpose.

CHAMBER · A
Forecast
What is about to happen.

The forward half. Macro calendar, central-bank bias, DXY, VIX, session clocks, correlated pairs, news windows, crowd positioning. The Lens asks: “given the next six hours, which instruments are in their edge window?” — and returns a framed answer, not a flood.

  • Calendar. Live macro, filtered to what touches the trader’s book
  • Bias. Central-bank, rate-path, trader’s own historical win-rate by regime
  • Session Clock. Tokyo · London · NY, against the trader’s edge by session
  • Crowd Sentiment. COT, retail positioning, social skew — when he opts in
  • Event Prep. A one-page brief for every scheduled event, auto-drafted
ONE EYE
+
ONE READ
CHAMBER · B
Analysis
What is already on the chart.

The structural half. Confluences, liquidity, BPRs, order blocks, fair-value gaps, pivots, round numbers, sessions. The Lens asks: “given what the chart is already showing, which Buy and Sell scenarios are live right now?” — and draws them, scored, with citations.

  • Nine Confluences. Named, iconed, with tests, status, confidence
  • Two Scenarios. One Buy, one Sell — drafted by AI, always both
  • Level Math. Entry, SL, TP, R·R, auto-sized to his risk rules
  • Why Tooltip. Every confluence carries a textbook explanation
  • History Modal. Hit rate of this exact confluence, this trader, last 90 days

F02 · III · THE ANALYSIS BUTTON

One amber button. One keystroke. Full AI read in under a second.

new CTA

The new CTA lives on the Forecast header, at the right edge of the symbol bar. It is not a tab — tabs are passive. The Analysis button is active: it forces the AI to do a full read of the chart currently on screen. Nine confluences scored. Two scenarios drafted. One AI confidence delivered. A short press triggers a fresh read; a long press pins the output to the right rail.

TRIGGER · SHORT PRESS
It is the “read this” button.

The trader taps it once. The Lens locks the current symbol, timeframe, and visible window, then runs every confluence detector, every liquidity read, every scenario drafter, every macro cross-check in parallel — and returns one structured object: a live Analysis.

The press is idempotent — tapping it twice gives the same answer as tapping it once, for as long as the chart does not move. The moment the trader changes timeframe or pair, the button pulses amber to say “a fresh read is available.”

A long press opens the Analysis in a drawer for review and annotation. A double-tap runs it in silent mode — the AI reads but doesn’t render the rail, feeding the result straight to the Brain for voice reply.

F02 · IV · CONFLUENCE LIBRARY

Nine named detectors. Every one scored. Every one cited.

09 confluences

The Lens ships with nine confluences in its standard library, each one a named detector running in parallel over the active chart. Every detector returns four things: status (forming, tested, confirmed, active), confidence (0–100), RR potential (scenario-dependent), and textbook explanation (a structured note the trader can tap to open). The library is extensible — a mentor can ship a private detector to his own room.

C·01
BPR Zone
Balanced Price Range

A range where price oscillates before rebalancing. The Lens marks its high, mid, and low, times its duration, and reports whether current price sits above or below it.

Status forming 75%
C·02
Weekly Open
Premium · Discount Pivot

The pivot that defines HTF bias for the week. The Lens streams the live weekly open, compares it to current price, and labels the market state — premium above, discount below.

Status tested 87%
C·03
Liquidity Sweep
Stop-Hunt Detection

Sharp probe through a prior high or low to trigger stops before the real move. The Lens identifies swept levels on weekly, daily, and Tokyo ranges, and scores the quality of the reclaim.

Status confirmed 90%
C·04
Pivot Lines
Daily R3—P—S3

Statistical levels derived from the prior session’s H/L/C — magnets and reversal zones the market respects. The Lens draws R3/R2/R1/P/S1/S2/S3 and flags the nearest active.

Status active 78%
C·05
Fair Value Gap
Displacement Inefficiency

A mispriced wick left behind by a strong displacement move. Price tends to revisit it to rebalance. The Lens marks HTF gaps, tracks first-touch, and confirms with LTF structure.

Status forming 72%
C·06
Order Block
Institutional Footprint

The last up/down candle before strong displacement — a mitigation zone where smart money accumulated. The Lens prioritises OBs that align with HTF bias and flags first-touch entries.

Status active 80%
C·07
Session Range
London · NY Killzones

Asia builds liquidity; London expands; NY continues or reverts. The Lens tracks session highs and lows, flags liquidity traps in Asia, and confirms expansion windows with the trader’s own historical session-edge.

Status tested 76%
C·08
200 EMA Bias
Dynamic Support / Resistance

The trend filter every desk watches. The Lens renders the 200 EMA across all open timeframes and labels HTF bias: above = bullish, below = bearish, paired with FVG/liquidity for entries.

Status active 69%
C·09
Round Numbers
Bank · Psychological Levels

The 00 and 50 handles attract liquidity. The Lens marks every round-number zone in the visible window, scores sweep-and-reclaim patterns, and uses them as partial and RR targets.

Status active 74%
F02 · V · SCENARIO ENGINE

Two scenarios, always. One Buy. One Sell. No hidden bias.

Buy · Sell

The Lens never shows a directional opinion without its opposite. Every run produces both a Buy scenario and a Sell scenario, each with its own entry window, stop, target, R:R, and AI confidence. The trader chooses — or declines both. The engine will not ship a single-sided read, ever. This is the structural guarantee that the AI cannot drift into becoming a signal group.

F02 · VI · THE CONFIDENCE PIPELINE

Six stages. Weighted. Deterministic. One number out.

06 stages

Every AI confidence score the Lens emits is the output of a six-stage pipeline. The score is not a vibe. It is a weighted function of six measurements that the trader can inspect, override, and export. If he does not trust the number, he can open the pipeline and see which stage reduced the confidence and by how much. No black box.

CONFIDENCE · pipeline How a score becomes a score v3.1 · seeded
01
Structureprice acts as context
Market structure read — higher highs / lower lows, break of structure, change of character. The highest-weighted stage, because nothing else matters if the chart is chopping.
24%
weight
02
Confluence Stackhow many agree
Count of active confluences, weighted by their individual confidence. Five 80%s beat one 95%. The Lens favours agreement across detectors over a single loud signal.
22%
weight
03
Historical Edgethis trader, this setup
The trader’s own 90-day win-rate on the exact confluence stack currently active. If he has never traded this stack, the stage pulls from the cohort; if the cohort is thin, the stage declares “low evidence”.
18%
weight
04
Macro Alignmentthe world behind the chart
Cross-check against DXY, yields, VIX, session phase, and scheduled events. A beautiful setup ten minutes before FOMC loses points; the same setup during quiet lunch holds them.
14%
weight
05
R:R Geometryis the math worth it
Minimum 1:2 to score anything; 1:3+ to score full. A high-conviction setup at 1:1 gets punished. The Lens will never serve a high confidence on poor geometry.
12%
weight
06
Trader Statethe man holding the mouse
Read of the trader’s current System-OS state (cortex, discipline, cooldown). If he is in a state where his own history says he executes this setup poorly, the confidence is marked but not hidden.
10%
weight

F02 · IX · KEYBOARD LANGUAGE

Twelve shortcuts. Every tab one keystroke away.

12 keys

The Lens is a desk tool. A trader must be able to run it with his hands on the keyboard while his eyes stay on the chart. Every frequently-used action has a chord, every chord composes, and the reference sheet is never more than ? away.

LENS SHORTCUTS · v1 Chord-based · consistent across deck and rail
