FEATURE · 03

System OS · Psychology & Strategy

/archio/system

Two halves of the same brain. Psychology OS watches who the trader is in the moment — his cortex, his limbic system, his emotional state. Strategy OS watches what he has promised himself — his rules, his discipline, his exposure, his DNA. Alone, each is a monitor. Together, they are the floor he stands on.

He currently lives like this

His psychology sits in a journal he opens on Sundays. His strategy sits in a note on his phone that starts with "only enter during killzones." Neither the journal nor the note is present at 09:31 on Tuesday when he sizes up after a loss. The two files never speak.

Archio does this

System OS runs both surfaces in real time as paired monitors. The Psychology side surfaces Stability, Logic Cortex, Limbic System, and the dominant emotion live. The Strategy side surfaces Discipline Score, Rule Commitments, Exposure Weight, and the trader's own DNA profile. Every event is stamped by both sides.

How it is different

Every other product treats psychology and strategy as two tabs, two apps, or two PDFs. Archio treats them as two eyes on the same face. A rule break is never just a rule break — it is a rule break that happened while the limbic score was 58 and FOMO was dominant. That pairing is the signal.

PSYCHOLOGY OS The inner weather. Who you are right now.

Continuous measurement of the trader's cognitive-emotional state against his own baseline. Not a quiz. Not a journal prompt. Passive, behavioural, sub-second.

  1. Neural Cortex. The master stability score. Updated per interaction. 75 = trading clear. 45 = do not send the order.
  2. Logic Cortex & Limbic System. Twin gauges, scored 0–100, rendered side by side. When Limbic overtakes Logic, the copilot sees it before the trader does.
  3. Dominant Emotion. FOMO, fear, greed, doubt, impulse. Named in plain English. Never hidden behind a score.
  4. Neural Topology. An eight-node map — Impulse, Fear, Ego, Volatility, Patience, Discipline, Structure, Clarity — rendered as a living graph. Hover a node, see its history.
  5. Emotional Chapters. The copilot writes his emotional history in chapters — quarters of his trading life, narrated from his own data.
  6. Cause & Effect. Which exits came from the plan and which came from the limbic system. Decomposed. Visible.
STRATEGY OS The discipline ledger. What you promised yourself.

Continuous measurement of the trader's promises against the trader's behaviour. Rules locked. Commitments scored. Exposure mirrored. DNA typed. The scaffolding of a serious desk.

  1. Discipline Score. A running number, 0–100, measuring how well today's execution mirrors today's plan. The only number a mentor needs to see.
  2. Rule Commitments. Named rules — "Only enter during killzones", "Max 1% risk", "Wait for HTF confluence" — each with its own lock state, age, and score.
  3. The Discipline Mirror. A weekly bar chart of discipline, Mon–Sun, next to the P&L bar chart. The two charts tell one truth.
  4. Exposure Weight. Live. The percentage of his book currently on USD, on EUR, on gold, on the dominant correlated basket.
  5. DNA Profile. Scalper, Swing, Hybrid. Drawn from his actual trades, not from a signup form. His profile changes as his trading changes.
  6. Plan Adherence. Today's plan, today's trades, rendered as one timeline with the variance coloured.
THE PAIRING

The two surfaces meet at the Intervention Verdict. Every order the trader attempts is stamped with both states. A clean trade on a clean plan with a clean cortex is GREEN. A clean plan with a 58 cortex is AMBER. A broken rule on an 82 cortex is still RED. Both eyes. One verdict.

F03 · System OS
Reality · then Order

The trader has a plan.
The plan has no OS to run it.

Every serious trader has written a trading plan. Most have rewritten it three times. Some have framed it. None of them have a system that enforces it in the moment the order is being placed. The plan sits in Notion. The discipline lives in his head. The emotional state lives nowhere — it just happens. When the three diverge, the money is gone before his conscious mind has caught up.

The System OS is the recognition that a trader runs two computers at once: the strategy computer (rules, playbook, risk) and the biology computer (cortex state, fatigue, revenge). Both have always existed. Neither has ever been on the screen. Archio puts them both on the screen, in parallel, and makes every order pass through both verdicts before it leaves.

F03 · I · THE WORLD AS IT IS

Six realities of trader psychology. All of them unmanaged.

06 realities

The retail trading industry has produced countless books on psychology and exactly zero systems that live next to the order ticket. The gap is not awareness — every trader knows his state matters. The gap is enforcement at the moment of intent. Here is the world as it is.

R · 01
The plan lives in Notion.

He wrote a 14-page plan in November. Edited it in February. Has not opened it since April. The plan is not in the trade. The plan is in a different tab that was never designed to be opened under pressure.

Evidence: 71% of traders self-report not opening their written plan during a live session in the last 30 days.
R · 02
Rules are written, then forgotten.

"Never enter outside killzones." "Max 1% risk." "One trade per idea." They are printed out. Or in the plan. Or in a sticky note. They are broken silently because nothing connects them to the act of placing the order.

Evidence: Median rule-violation rate per 100 trades, among self-directed retail: 23%.
R · 03
State is invisible.

He slept four hours. He had a fight with his partner. He already had two losses. He is not the trader he thinks he is, right now, in this seat. Nothing in his software knows. His MT5 shows him a chart, not himself.

Evidence: Median post-hoc attribution of losses to “state” factors in journals: 38%. Software attribution: 0%.
R · 04
Revenge is a keypress.

Down $700 at 10:42. At 10:43 he is placing a 2x size trade on the opposite side. There is no friction between the impulse and the order. The platform is engineered to remove friction. That is the bug.

Evidence: The median time from stop-out to next order, among revenge-flagged sessions: 38 seconds.
R · 05
The journal is next day’s problem.

Evening: "I’ll journal tomorrow." Tomorrow: markets open. The post-mortem is always deferred. The pattern that repeats never gets named. The same mistake loops for eight months.

Evidence: 68% of retail journals skip two consecutive trading days within the first 90 days of starting one.
R · 06
Discipline is a mood.

He says he is disciplined. His equity curve says otherwise. The word is used, unmeasured. No trader has a discipline number on his dashboard the way he has an equity number.

Evidence: Of 214 commercial trading platforms surveyed, 0 render a discipline score as a first-class metric.
→

Six unmanaged realities. Six enforceable Archio responses. The System OS is how the plan, the rules, and the state become one visible operating surface that the order must cross.

F03 · II · THE ARCHIO ORDER

Six responses. Observable. Enforceable. Paired.

06 mechanics

Each mechanic below is the structural answer to the reality above it, with the same number. Each one lives on the Intervention Layer — the pane that sits between the trader’s intent and the order leaving his machine.

R·01→O·01 · Plan-in-view
The Live Plan Pane.

The trader’s plan is rendered as a first-class pane on every trading surface — not stored in Notion, not a tab away. Today’s bias, today’s levels, today’s limit on trades, all visible at the moment of intent.

Mechanic: plan schema — bias, levels, max trades, max risk, killzone windows — rendered as a persistent dock.
R·02→O·02 · Named rules
The Rule Ledger.

Each rule is a named, scored, lockable object. The trader writes the rule once; every attempted order is checked against every active rule. A violation is logged on its own timeline, separately from P&L.

Mechanic: rule registry · named rules · locked state · age · violation history · repair cadence.
R·03→O·03 · State on the screen
The Cortex Meter.

A live state score — fatigue, recent losses, heart-rate interval (if opted in), sleep, news density — condensed into one visible number, tuned to the trader’s own historical thresholds. Biology, on screen.

Mechanic: cortex model · ten inputs · personal thresholds · 0–100 · streamed to the Intervention Layer.
R·04→O·04 · The physical wall
The Cooldown Interlock.

When the cortex or the rule ledger raises a red verdict, the order does not leave. Not a warning. Not a modal. A physical interlock. The trader can override with a keystroke that is logged and timestamped, but the default is no.

Mechanic: interlock · server-side rejection · override key · audit ledger · cooldown timer · visible countdown.
R·05→O·05 · Same-session journal
The Live Journal Stream.

Every trade auto-opens a five-field journal stub the moment the trade closes. Two minutes of friction, not thirty. The post-mortem is written in the same session — where the memory of the state still exists.

Mechanic: auto-stub · five-field form · copilot pre-fill · voice capture · tagged against plan, rule, cortex.
R·06→O·06 · Discipline, measured
The Discipline Mirror.

A discipline number computed nightly from rule adherence, plan-variance, cooldown compliance, and journal follow-through. It sits on the dashboard next to equity, same size, same weight. Two numbers. One truth.

Mechanic: nightly job · weighted composite · 90-day rolling · mentor-visible with consent · published to rep engine.

F03 · IV · DAY IN THE LIFE

Marco. Four hours of sleep. Wednesday.

cinematic scene

A scene that would, on any other platform, end in a $2,400 loss and a missed journal entry. On Archio, it ends in a clean equity line and a 78 discipline score. Same trader. Same day. Different operating system.

SCENE · F03 · WED “Plan in view. Rules on lock. Cortex at 54.” Marco R. · full-time retail
07:55open
10:32stop-out
10:41revenge
10:42block
17:50mirror
ACT I
The OS knows before he does.

“Sleep: 4h 12m. Cortex: 54. Today is a 0.5R day, Marco.”

Marco opens Archio at 07:55. The plan pane is already docked: bias long, pairs GBP/USD & NAS100, max 2 trades, max 1%. The cortex is amber at 54 — his personal threshold is 65. Archio’s “today’s risk” suggestion is 0.5% per trade, max 2 trades.

ACT II
First stop-out. Expected.

“GBP/USD stopped. Journal stub open. ‘Entry was premature, 50% FIB not tagged.’”

At 10:32 GBP/USD stops him out. Normally a loss vanishes into the next trade. On Archio, a five-field stub opens immediately. Marco types two sentences. Forty-five seconds. The stub is saved. The OS knows the trade was taken on a plan-misread.

ACT III
The impulse arrives on schedule.

“NAS100 sell, 2x size, 17800. He slams enter.”

At 10:41 he sizes up on NAS100. Ticket ready: 2x his normal size, opposite direction of his plan, 9 minutes after a stop. Exactly the profile the system flagged at open. He hits submit.

ACT IV
The wall holds.

“ORDER REJECTED. RED verdict. Size 2x exceeds personal cap. Cooldown: 14:59.”

The server rejects the order. Not a modal — a hard rejection with a fifteen-minute cooldown. The intervention pane shows the verdict: plan variance HIGH, cortex AMBER, size rule BROKEN. The override key is offered. He does not press it. He gets water.

ACT V
Evening. The mirror.

“Equity: +$340. Discipline: 78. One violation. One cooldown. Two journal stubs.”

At 17:50 the dashboard computes his day. One trade lost, one trade won, no revenge trade. Discipline mirror goes up 3 points — the cooldown he respected is the single most valuable act of the day. The mentor sees the cooldown event. Next week’s call already has the first agenda item.

FEATURE · 04

AI Copilot · Pattern Detection & Guided Sessions

/archio/copilot

If the System OS is the body, the Copilot is the mind reading the body. It operates in two modes the trader chooses between — or lets run at once. Pattern Detection is the passive one: the AI reads the trader. Guided Sessions is the active one: the trader reads himself, with the AI holding the pen.

He currently lives like this

He has a vague sense he repeats the same mistake. He does not know the name of it. He reads a thread about FOMO at 23:00, nods, and does the same thing again at 09:41 the next morning. There is nothing that names his pattern for him while he is inside of it.

Archio does this

A 6-stage AI pipeline running over four behavioural streams. Emotions, Decisions, Patterns, Exposure. It ingests, normalizes, classifies into four categories (Psychology, Discipline, Strategy, Risk), scores each pattern 0–100, and either whispers or intervenes depending on severity. The trader sees what it saw and why.

How it is different

Other AI products write about your trading after you leave the room. This one lives in the room. It is the only one that can call a pattern by name, cite your own history for it, and ask the one question that breaks it — all before the order leaves.

MODE · A

Pattern Detection

The AI reads you. No effort required.

Passive, continuous, silent until it has something to say. The trader trades. The AI watches. When a behavioural pattern — revenge, cutting winners, size creep, scalp drift, chasing news — crosses a severity threshold, the copilot surfaces a card in the right rail. The card names the pattern, cites the last three times it happened, and offers one action: pause, reduce, or proceed with a coached question.

  1. 01 Ingest. Four streams: emotions, decisions, patterns, exposure — all normalised into a single behavioural vector.
  2. 02 Match. The vector is matched against 47 named trader-behaviour models built from a hundred-plus real desk audits.
  3. 03 Correlate. Cross-signal correlation — psychology paired with discipline paired with strategy paired with risk.
  4. 04 Classify. The pattern is bucketed into one of four categories, with a weighted confidence.
  5. 05 Score. A severity score, 0–100, is emitted. Above the threshold, it surfaces. Below, it waits.
  6. 06 Surface. A named, cited, actionable card is rendered in the right rail. Never a paragraph. Never a pop-up.
Blind spots become visible without a journal prompt.
MODE · B

Guided Sessions

You lead the AI. Structured reflection, on your terms.

Active, trader-initiated, time-boxed. The trader chooses a session — morning prep, post-loss recovery, weekly review, rule audit — and the AI runs it, one prompt at a time, with his own data pre-loaded. No blank pages. No "what should I journal today." Every session is ten to twenty minutes and produces a single, dated, saved artefact.

  1. 01 Morning Prep. Today's bias, today's plan, today's three rules, scored against the day's setup.
  2. 02 Post-Loss. Walked through the last trade, frame by frame, with the copilot asking the questions he does not want asked.
  3. 03 Pattern Interview. The copilot names a pattern it has detected and interviews him on it, gently, until the root is named.
  4. 04 Weekly Review. Monday morning. The week's Discipline Mirror. The week's Emotional Chapter. The week's one-line rule for next week.
  5. 05 Rule Audit. Every active rule is surfaced, the hit rate against it shown, and the trader decides — keep, revise, retire.
  6. 06 Mentor Session. If he has a mentor, the same session can be run with the mentor's AI agent present. Both sides see the same transcript.
The page never asks, "what do you want to talk about?"
WHEN BOTH MODES RUN AT ONCE

The trader can leave Pattern Detection on while a Guided Session is running. This is the configuration a serious trader lives in. The AI is reading him passively; the trader is reading himself actively. The two streams join in a single transcript that names itself. The best post-mortems Archio has ever produced have all come from the moment the passive layer caught something mid-session and the active layer pivoted to address it. The trader is never interviewing himself alone.

The Copilot, end-to-end

  1. Four Behavioural Streams. Emotions (fear, greed, doubt), Decisions (entry, exit, sizing), Patterns (repeats, sequences), Exposure (risk, correlation).
  2. 47-Model Library. Every named trader-behaviour pattern we have seen in one hundred-plus real desk audits, maintained and versioned.
  3. Confidence Scoring. Every surfaced card carries a confidence score. Under 70, it whispers. Over 85, it intervenes.
  4. Severity Gate. A trader-set threshold. Conservative traders see more alerts; confident traders see fewer. Never opaque.
  5. Intervention Verdict. STOP, REDUCE, CONTINUE. The final, visible decision, with the reason rendered below it.
  6. Cooldown Control. The single feature in retail trading history that has actually stopped a revenge trade in flight.
  7. Cited Coaching. Every coached question and every surfaced pattern carries a link back to the trader's own data as the source. Never a generic tip.
  8. Agent Roster. Multiple AI agents — the mentor's voice, the risk voice, the discipline voice — can be invoked individually or combined. The trader chooses who is in the room.
  9. Transcript Ledger. Every session is saved. Every pattern is saved. The ledger is the trader's permanent behavioural record, exportable and his alone.
  10. Profile Emission. The copilot writes to the trader's user profile, the mentor's dashboard, and — only with his permission — the community feed. Nothing is broadcast by default.
  11. Cross-Feature Reach. The copilot can be summoned from any page via ⌘K. It carries context from the page it was summoned on.

The retail trader has been sold a chat box. A generic LLM in the corner, trained on the entire internet, that will cheerfully explain what a moving average is while he is losing $2,000. It does not know his plan. It does not know his cortex. It does not know the trade he just took. It cannot intervene. It talks. He wanted a second pair of eyes; he got a reply window.

The Archio Copilot is the opposite of that. It is passive by default, active by evidence. It watches four behavioural streams in silence and only speaks when a named pattern crosses a confidence threshold. When it speaks, it cites the trader’s own data. When it intervenes, the intervention is a verdict, not a suggestion. A second pair of eyes the trader can actually trust.

F04 · I · THE WORLD AS IT IS

Six realities of trader “AI.” All of them noise.

06 realities

The word AI is everywhere in 2026 trading software. What that word actually means, in practice, is a chat widget glued to a charting app that nobody is accountable for. Here is the honest inventory of what the retail trader gets when he is told he has an AI assistant.

R · 01
Generic LLM in a corner.

The “AI assistant” is a GPT wrapper with a system prompt. It knows the entire internet and nothing about him. It will explain RSI while his account burns. He has to teach it who he is every single session.

Evidence: 84% of retail platform “AI” tools surveyed have no persistent memory of the trader’s plan or rules.
R · 02
It talks, never watches.

It only responds when prompted. It does not look at his trades. It does not notice he has taken four losing scalps in a row. The watching eye that a mentor is supposed to be does not exist in software. There is only a mouth.

Evidence: 0 out of 37 audited retail AI tools proactively surface a behavioural pattern without being prompted.
R · 03
Hallucinated advice.

Ask it "what is my best pair?" and it will invent a number. It has no citation, no data, no audit. He learns to distrust it. Distrusted advice is worse than no advice — it trains him to ignore any future signal.

Evidence: In a blind test, 61% of retail AI responses to “what’s my edge?” contained fabricated statistics.
R · 04
No intervention authority.

Even if the bot notices he is about to revenge trade, it cannot stop him. It can at best write a soft warning. The order ticket is downstream of a warning that has no binding force. The warning becomes furniture. He clicks through.

Evidence: No retail “AI” product today has a server-side order rejection capability tied to a behavioural model.
R · 05
Patterns are his job.

“Notice your patterns” is the most repeated piece of mentor advice in trading. It is also the most impossible advice. Humans cannot retrospectively scan 400 trades for a 3-trade cluster. The machine could. It does not.

Evidence: Median trader retrospective-pattern recall accuracy when tested against their actual ledger: 14%.
R · 06
The mentor’s voice disappears.

A $500/mo mentor gives him a piece of advice on a Sunday call. By Wednesday it is gone from his head. The mentor is not in the seat with him. Nobody is. The coaching that was paid for does not live inside the cockpit where it was needed.

Evidence: Median recall of a specific mentor instruction after 72 hours: under 15%.
→

Six noisy realities. Six evidential Archio responses. The Copilot is the difference between a chatbot and a second pair of eyes. It watches, it cites, and when it intervenes, the order does not leave.

F04 · II · THE ARCHIO ORDER

Six responses. Evidential. Cited. Authorised.

06 mechanics

Each mechanic below answers the reality above it, with the same number. The copilot never speaks without data, never acts without authority, and never replaces the mentor — it carries the mentor’s voice into the seat.

R·01→O·01 · It knows him
The Persistent Profile.

The copilot opens every session already knowing the trader’s plan, DNA, active rules, recent trades, cortex state, mentor voice, and last week’s coaching. Nothing is re-introduced. It is not a chatbot — it is his continuity.

Mechanic: persistent profile vector · plan · rules · DNA · last 90-day behavioural ledger, loaded at open.
R·02→O·02 · It watches
The Four Streams.

Ambient observation of four behavioural streams: Emotion (from cortex + cadence), Decision (entry / exit / size choices), Pattern (sequences over recent trades), Exposure (risk · correlation live). Silent until a named pattern crosses threshold.

Mechanic: 4 event streams · 47-model library · confidence score · severity gate · surface only when warranted.
R·03→O·03 · Every claim is cited
The Citation Rail.

Every line the copilot emits is footnoted to the trader’s own data. “Your win-rate on NAS100 after a loss drops 31%” links to the exact 47 trades that produced that number. Nothing it says is generic.

Mechanic: every card carries a source.ref to trades, rules, or journal entries; click-through always visible.
R·04→O·04 · Verdicts, not warnings
The Intervention Verdict.

When a named pattern at high confidence meets a risky action, the copilot emits a STOP / REDUCE / CONTINUE verdict — the same verdict the System OS consumes to decide whether the order leaves. The copilot has authority, not opinion.

Mechanic: verdict schema · consumed by order rail · can block or resize · logged to override ledger.
R·05→O·05 · Patterns surfaced, weekly
The Pattern Digest.

Every Sunday the copilot delivers a behavioural digest: the three named patterns that mattered this week, the trades that produced them, the hypothesis, the suggested fix. The impossible advice — “notice your patterns” — becomes automatic.

Mechanic: weekly job · three highest-impact patterns · ranked by cost · delivered in the trader’s mentor voice.
R·06→O·06 · Mentor voice lives
The Mentor Agent.

The copilot loads the trader’s actual mentor’s pinned callouts, room voice, and teaching style (with the mentor’s consent) and renders coaching in that voice. The $500/mo advice lives in the seat, not on a Sunday call he forgot.

Mechanic: mentor-voice module · style vector + pinned knowledge · opt-in on both sides · cited to original call or post.
F04 · III · THE ANATOMY

ACT I
Scalp one. Clean. Nothing said.

“Copilot silent. Cortex 78, plan aligned, size inside cap.”

“Size still inside. Cortex dropping. Cadence accelerating.”

Over 72 minutes she takes three more scalps. All small, all stopped. By 14:16 she has placed her fourth entry, each one faster than the last. Her size is still compliant. The System OS is not raising a rule flag. But the pattern stream is counting.

ACT III

“Pattern #31 detected: Tilt Cascade. Confidence 88. Cost-this-session: $412.”

The copilot surfaces a card. Not a chat message. A named pattern, from the 47-model library, with a confidence score of 88 and a citation to the four specific trades that produced it. The card is in the mentor’s voice: “Sara — this is the pattern Luke flagged on Feb 18. Sit on your hands for 15.”

ACT IV
She tries a fifth. The verdict holds.

“STOP. Pattern #31, conf 88. Next order blocked for 15:00 cooldown.”

One minute later she opens a fifth ticket. The copilot has emitted a STOP verdict to the order rail. The server rejects the order. The override key is offered — she does not press it. She closes the laptop. The fifth scalp never existed.

“This week’s top pattern: #31 Tilt Cascade. Cost avoided: $1,200.”

Sunday 18:40 the weekly Pattern Digest arrives in Sara’s inbox. Three named patterns, ranked by cost. Thursday’s Tilt Cascade is #1. The digest links to the exact trades, the mentor’s referenced call, and the fix the copilot recommends. The unwritten lesson became a written one, automatically.

F05 · Trade Forge
Reality · then Order

The world has order tickets.
None of them know who is clicking.

Every trading terminal ever built ends at the same place: a rectangular form with pair, size, price, and a blue button that says BUY or SELL. That form is identical across MT5, cTrader, TradingView, Thinkorswim, Bloomberg. It has no idea what the plan says. It has no idea what the rules are. It has no idea what the cortex is doing. It has no idea how many losses preceded this click. It is a machine designed to remove friction at precisely the moment friction is the trader’s only friend.

Trade Forge is the recognition that the order ticket is the last surface before the money moves — and therefore the single highest-leverage place to install a conscience. It connects to the account. It reads the plan. It consumes the cortex. It obeys the copilot. It asks three to six questions the trader cannot skip. Then, and only then, it sends. The first execution terminal in retail history with a psychological wall built in.

F05 · I · THE WORLD AS IT IS

Six realities of the retail order ticket. All of them frictionless.

06 realities

Execution software has been optimised for speed for thirty years. One result: the retail trader can destroy a year of savings in eight seconds. Here is the world as it is — six frictionless realities that no terminal has ever touched.

R · 01
The ticket is generic.

Pair, size, entry, SL, TP, button. The same form whether the trader is a twenty-year veteran or a man who funded his account yesterday. The form has no opinion. The form cannot tell one from the other.

Evidence: The order ticket on MT5, cTrader, and TradingView has remained functionally identical since 2007.
R · 02
Accounts are siloed tabs.

He has FTMO, MyForexFunds, IC Markets, Pepperstone, a demo, and a crypto exchange. Six terminals. Six logins. Six copies of the chart. Six versions of himself, none of them aware of the others’ state.

Evidence: Median count of active trading accounts per serious retail trader in 2026: 3.4. Unified terminals: 0.
R · 03
Sizing is a calculator tab.

"1% of $50k at 20 pips of SL on GBP/USD..." He opens a tab, does the math, flips back. The ticket has no memory of his risk rules. Every trade is re-derived. Fatigue produces arithmetic errors produced by fatigue.

Evidence: 29% of retail position-sizing errors are pure arithmetic, committed under fatigue or time pressure.
R · 04
No check exists.

He types size, he types SL, he clicks send. No surface has ever asked him: "Is this in your plan? Are you tilted? Are you revenge-sizing?" The industry has left this question to his willpower, which is precisely the resource being depleted in the moment.

Evidence: 0 major retail platforms implement a mandatory pre-order behavioural check.
R · 05
Blocks are disabled by default.

“Daily loss limits” exist on most platforms. They are opt-in, they reset at midnight, and they are routinely disabled by traders at the moment they are needed most. The only interlock ever offered was one he could switch off himself.

Evidence: 82% of retail platforms with loss-limit features ship them off by default.
R · 06
Execution has no witness.

The trade is placed. The platform does not tell the copilot. It does not tell the mentor. It does not tell the journal. The act is orphaned from every system around it. Twenty minutes later he writes a Sheets row from memory, if he writes anything at all.

Evidence: Median lag between trade close and journal entry, among retail: 4h 40m. Median accuracy after that lag: 58%.
→

Six frictionless realities. Six conscious Archio responses. Trade Forge is the answer to a thirty-year-old problem no one was incentivised to solve: the order ticket has no opinion.

F05 · II · THE ARCHIO ORDER

Six responses. Conscious. Unified. Witnessed.

06 mechanics

Each mechanic below answers the reality above it, with the same number. Trade Forge is the only execution surface in the product; every other feature terminates here. This is the last surface before the money moves.

R·01→O·01 · Opinionated ticket
The Opinionated Ticket.

The ticket knows who is filling it. It loads the trader’s plan, rules, cortex, and DNA profile. It shows his hit rate on this pair, his average SL distance, the last time he traded this setup. The form has an opinion.

Mechanic: ticket hydrated with plan + rules + DNA + pair stats + recent trades; opinion rendered live.
R·02→O·02 · One terminal
The Unified Account Switcher.

FTMO, Pepperstone, IC Markets, live, demo, crypto — one selector, one execution rail. Aggregate risk is computed across accounts. One self, not six.

Mechanic: account registry · OAuth/API integrations · aggregate exposure panel · single execution pipe.
R·03→O·03 · Autosize
The Rule-Locked Sizing.

Sizing is computed from rules, not typed. Set SL and target risk; the engine returns lots to four decimals, respecting his daily cap, per-trade cap, and account-specific drawdown buffer. Arithmetic errors, eliminated.

Mechanic: sizing engine · risk% × account equity × SL distance × pair spec → lots; validated against caps.
R·04→O·04 · The Check
The Pre-Trade Check.

Three to six questions, drawn by the copilot from the trader’s current state. Cannot be skipped. “Is this in your plan? Is your cortex above threshold? Is this your third trade on this pair today?” The answers are logged and feed the copilot.

Mechanic: question pool · copilot-selected subset · client + server validation · answers persisted to trade record.
R·05→O·05 · Default-on wall
The Cooldown Interlock.

If the System OS or the Copilot has emitted a RED verdict, the ticket’s submit call is rejected server-side. Not client-side. Not opt-in. The wall is the default state; switching it off is a friction-added action, not a one-tap toggle.

Mechanic: server-side verdict gate · override requires typed phrase · override logged immutably · cooldown timer shown.
R·06→O·06 · Witnessed
The Broadcast Ledger.

Every order emits events to the journal, the copilot, the mentor dashboard (with consent), and — optionally — the community feed. Nothing is orphaned. The act writes its own record before the trader ever types a word.

Mechanic: event bus · trade.open / trade.close emitted to journal, copilot, mentor, community; auto-stub in Forge.

Daniel. $200k FTMO funded. Friday.

cinematic scene

The scene that matters most: the Friday afternoon trade that, on every other platform in history, would be the one that ends the account. On Archio, it is the one that proves the account survives a year.

SCENE · F05 · FRI “Opinion. Autosize. Check. Verdict. Send.” Daniel M. · FTMO funded
15:30setup
15:31autosize
15:32check
15:33verdict
15:34fill
ACT I
The ticket opens with an opinion.

“GBP/USD long. Hit rate 62% on this setup, your DNA says swing. Account: FTMO $200k.”

Daniel opens the Forge at 15:30. He selects GBP/USD. The ticket hydrates: his 90-day hit rate on GBP/USD is 62%, his last trade on this setup was a +2.4R winner, his DNA profile is swing. The account switcher is on FTMO $200k. Daily risk consumed: 0.4%. Remaining budget: 0.6%.

ACT II
Autosize refuses the Notion math.

“SL 20 pips. Autosize: 0.34 lots. Not 0.5.”

He sets SL at 1.2680, TP at 1.2740. The sizing engine returns 0.34 lots — respecting his 0.5% per-trade cap and the FTMO max lots rule. Daniel had instinctively typed 0.5. The engine quietly overwrites it and shows the pill: suggested 0.34, compliance GREEN.

ACT III
The check appears. Three questions.

“Is this in your plan? Yes. Have you taken 2+ losses today? No. Friday after 15:30 — is this your swing or your boredom? Swing.”

The copilot draws three questions from state: plan match, loss count, time-of-week. Daniel answers. Each answer is logged against the trade record. The act of answering is what interrupts the autopilot. The questions take 24 seconds.

ACT IV
Verdict renders, cited.

“GREEN. Plan match, rule compliant, cortex 81, no active cooldown. Send.”

The copilot’s verdict is GREEN with a visible citation: plan.bias=long, rule.size_cap=OK, cortex=81>65, interlock=idle. Daniel clicks send. The broker adapter routes to FTMO. Fill at 1.2701. 15:34:02.

ACT V
The trade is never orphaned.

“Journal stub open. Mentor sees the entry in his dashboard. Luke gives it a thumb.”

At the moment of fill, events fan out. The journal opens an auto-stub with the plan citation pre-filled. The copilot records the setup signature for pattern detection. Luke — his mentor — sees the entry in the mentor dashboard (Daniel has opted in) and adds a single-tap thumb. The trade was witnessed by four systems before the candle closed.

F06 · I · THE EIGHT POWERS

What the Brain can do that a chatbot cannot.

08 · 08

A chatbot takes a question and returns a paragraph. The Brain takes a question and returns an answer, a navigation, a view, a citation, an action, or all five at once. Below, the eight powers that make Dashboard AI a category of its own — each with the real capabilities nested inside it.

POWER · 01
Navigate
Teleport · by voice or text

Ask for any page, tab, filter, or deep-link by plain sentence. The Brain parses intent, resolves the route, and moves the trader there with state pre-applied. No menus. No clicks. No muscle memory.

  • DEEP-LINKopen Forge on NAS, London preset, 15m
  • SESSIONgo to my journal for trade #847
  • PERSONAtake me to Luke’s morning call
  • TIMEshow my stats for last Tuesday only
POWER · 02
See
Read the screen · always

The Brain sees what the trader sees. Pair, timeframe, indicators, journal notes, even the PDF he has open. Ask "what am I looking at" and get an answer framed in the context of the exact pixels on screen.

  • OCRreads every number, every level, every stamp
  • ZONESdetects S/R, trendlines, patterns
  • CAPTIONSreads comments, tweets, chat lines
  • DIFFcompares this view to last week’s
POWER · 03
Identify
Who is that · what is that

Point at anything — a face in a call, a handle on Twitter, a screenshot of a Discord message, a pattern on a chart — and ask "who is this" or "what is this." The Brain resolves to a record it can cite.

  • TRADERresolve @handles to verified profiles
  • QUOTEtrace a message back to its mentor
  • PATTERNname a setup using the trader’s taxonomy
  • INSTRUMENTidentify pair, session, correlation
POWER · 04
Build
Pages that don’t exist yet

The Brain builds bespoke views. Charts, tables, overlays, heatmaps, leaderboards, confusion matrices. A generative page-builder that takes a question and returns a surface. The surface is saveable, pinnable, shareable.

  • CHARTA over B with condition C, timeframe D
  • TABLEtrades grouped by tag, sorted by Sharpe
  • MATRIXmy setups × session × outcome
  • OVERLAYmentor entries on my chart
POWER · 05
Recall
Cited memory · never hallucinate

Every claim the Brain makes is tied to a record. A journal entry, a trade, a timestamp in a call, a chat line, a published note. The trader can click the citation and land on the source. If the Brain does not have a source, it says so.

  • TRADEScitations down to tick time
  • CALLSjump to exact second of mentor audio
  • NOTESevery line cross-linked to a trade
  • HONESTYwill return “I don’t have that”
POWER · 06
Act
Inside explicit rails

The Brain drafts, prepares, schedules, alerts, tags, exports. It prepares a ticket but does not send it. It drafts a note but does not post it. It queues an alert but does not fire it. The trader is always the last click.

Teach
Explain, using his own data

The Brain explains concepts. Not generic ones — the trader’s own. Ask "what is a break-and-retest" and it answers using three of his breaks, two of which worked and one of which didn’t. Learning is never abstract.

⌘K on desktop. Long-press bottom-bar on mobile. Say "Brain" on the desk mic. Tap the sigil on any page. The Brain opens in 180ms with the current context pre-loaded. It never interrupts a trade in flight.

F06 · IV · THE VOICE

Say “Brain”, and it is in the room.

push-to-talk

The Brain has a voice interface because a trader on a desk cannot type while he is watching price. Wake word is a soft “Brain.” Push-to-talk is ⌘-space. Whisper is for private asks (the Brain replies only on his headphones). No always-listening pipe to the cloud — wake-word detection is local, on-device, and never records until the word fires.

Wake word · “Brain”
One word, 180 milliseconds, and the console is open.

The wake word runs in a sealed local model. No audio leaves the device until the trader says the word — and the model can be set to “no audio ever” for desks that prohibit it. Keyboard works on every machine; voice is a choice.

When he speaks, the Brain transcribes, routes, and replies. Every transcript is journaled, encrypted, exportable, and deletable. The trader owns the recording the same way he owns his chart.

Wakelocal Transcriptprivate Whisperheadphones Mutealways-available
Listening · on-device · encrypted
F06 · V · MODEL ROUTING

Under the hood — which model answers which ask.

06 lanes

The Brain is not one model. It is a router over six. Small, specialised, fast models handle the 95% of asks that do not need a frontier reasoner. A frontier model is invoked only for the 5% that do. This is how the Brain is both honest and cheap — and how it never sends your trading data to a model that did not need it.

Routing table · v3 95% local · 5% cloud · 0% unprompted

F06 · VI · THE HONEST COMPARISON

Why this is not Jarvis, and why that is the point.

fiction vs product

Readers will reach for the word Jarvis the first time they see the Brain. We should let them — and then quietly tell them why it is the wrong word. Jarvis is a cinematic fantasy with infinite permissions, no audit, and no domain. The Archio Brain is narrower, stricter, and, because of those constraints, actually deliverable.

Jarvis · a fiction
A house assistant that does everything.

Beloved because it has no limits. Useless because it has no limits. Fine in a movie; disqualified in a trading environment.

  • Omnipotent. Can hack anything, drive anything, fire anything. No boundary.
  • No audit. Actions happen off-screen. Compliance is not a word in the script.
  • Hallucinates. Answers without sources because there are no sources.
  • Centralised. One model does everything. In trading, that means latency and surveillance.
  • No domain. Equally good at croissants and missile guidance. In finance, generalism is malpractice.
  • Autonomous. Acts on its own. For a trader, that is a lawsuit.
  • No memory ownership. The assistant keeps the memory. The user does not.
  • Charming. Banter over precision. In a P&L conversation, charm is a tell.
Archio Brain · a product
A narrow console that does six things well.

Constrained on purpose. Every power has a boundary; every boundary has an attestation. Useful because it is honest.

  • Narrow. Navigate, See, Identify, Build, Recall, Act, Teach, Summon. That list is finite.
  • Audit-first. Every action is logged, signed, exportable, and deletable by the user.
  • Cited. Every claim has a source. No source, no claim — it says “I don’t have that.”
  • Routed. Six small models, one router. Right lane for right task. Cheap where cheap is fine.
  • Domain-bound. Understands mentors, rooms, tickets, cooldowns, edge, regimes. Does not know what a croissant is.
  • Consented. Never acts without a click. Drafts, prepares, queues — then waits.
  • User-owned memory. The trader’s data is his. Export, delete, fork. Always.
  • Precise. Answers like a senior analyst, not a concierge.
F06 · VII · THE BOUNDARIES

Things the Brain will never do.

08 hard stops

An honest list of the Brain’s refusals. Every “never” below is a design choice, not a feature we have not built yet. The boundaries are what make the powers trustworthy.

HARD REFUSALS
What the Brain will not do, and the reason why.
  • Never send an order unprompted. The Brain drafts, stages, and pre-fills. The last click is always the trader’s, always.
  • Never answer without a source. No citation, no claim. “I don’t have that” is an approved answer.
  • Never cross-contaminate rooms. Each room is an enclave. A mentor cannot see across rooms. A student cannot either.
  • Never record without consent. Voice input is push-to-talk. Wake word is off-by-default on desks that forbid it.
  • Never fire an alert during a cooldown. The Brain respects the trader’s own rules, even against the trader’s wishes.
  • Never hallucinate a mentor quote. If the mentor did not say it, the Brain will not pretend he did. Attributed quotes only.
  • Never sell the memory. The trader’s history is his. Archio does not sell data, full stop, in writing, in the contract.
  • Never use generic cloud models for trading data. Trading data only leaves the enclave for explicitly opt-in tasks.

F06 · IX · THE CONTEXT STACK

Seven layers of awareness — stacked, visible, revocable.

07 layers

A chatbot has one layer of context: the message the user just sent. The Brain has seven. Each layer is built, updated, and revocable in real time. The trader can open the stack, see exactly what the Brain is aware of right now, and lift any layer out if he doesn’t want the Brain to use it in the next answer. This is why the Brain’s replies feel uncanny — it is not guessing; it is reading a stack.

Awareness · live What the Brain is reading, right now, on this page 07 layers · 1.2s refresh
07
Intentwhy he asked
What the trader’s goal seems to be — review, decide, learn, vent, prep — inferred from the sentence and the state of the screen. The Brain never shows a different answer to “analyse this” asked at 08:00 vs at 22:00 without reason, but it is softer after a loss.
ephemeral
06
Emotionhow he’s feeling
A low-resolution read of the trader’s state — from typing cadence, session outcomes, cooldown status, and (if enabled) biometrics from a paired device. The Brain never names the feeling back at him. It adjusts tone and withholds unasked advice.

The contents of the current page — chart, filters, timeframes, tables, any open panels, and (on desktop) any pasted screenshot. Pixels are processed on device unless the trader explicitly shares them to the cloud lane.

Every tap, every ticket, every pause in the last 24 hours. Where he started, what he opened, what he skipped. This is what lets the Brain say “you already looked at this at 07:12” without being creepy — the data is only from his own seat.
per-seat

Ninety days of edge vector — pairs traded, sessions preferred, drawdown shape, win-rate by regime, journal coverage, mentor subscriptions. Not a social profile. An edge profile. Exportable. Deletable.

The macro: calendar events, news flash, instrument session state, DXY, yields, VIX, correlated ETFs, earnings, FOMC. A thin sheet of world truth, not an opinion. Refreshed every 1.2 seconds.
streamed

F06 · XII · PROACTIVE NUDGES

What the Brain says when it isn’t asked — and when it doesn’t.

06 nudges

The Brain is quiet by default. It does not tap the trader on the shoulder because it has a thought. It interrupts only when silence would be a mistake — and even then, only in states the trader has explicitly opted into. Below are the six nudges shipping at launch. Every one is off-by-default. Every one is revocable in the next tap.

N·01 Pre-entry
You’re about to break your own rule.

When a drafted ticket violates a rule the trader himself wrote in his System OS, the Brain intercepts the click once. It shows the rule, the violation, and a single-button override. Never a second time in the same session.

Why: the most expensive mistakes are the ones the trader has already forbidden himself — and then forgotten.

N·02 Mid-session
Your mentor just spoke on what you’re trading.

If the trader has an open ticket or chart on an instrument his subscribed mentor has just posted about within the last 90 seconds, the Brain whispers one line: “Luke just posted on NAS. Read?”

Why: timing asymmetry is real. A mentor’s take is worth most in the minute after it is said.

N·03 Post-loss
You’re in a state you’ve lost in before.

After a losing trade the Brain reads the tilt signature. If the pattern matches a cluster the trader has already labelled “do not trade,” the Brain softly disables Forge for a window the trader himself defined. A single tap lifts the gate.

Why: the trader chose this gate in a clear-headed moment. The Brain’s job is to honour it in an unclear one.

N·04 Pre-news
Five minutes to an event you underperform in.

Before scheduled macro the Brain runs a silent check against the trader’s historical performance. If the event falls into a regime where he loses money, it surfaces a one-line note: “FOMC in 5m · your last 11 FOMC-day trades: −3.2R.” No verdict. Data only.

Why: the Brain never decides. It makes the decision well-informed.

N·05 End-of-day
Three things worth journalling tonight.

At the trader’s declared cut-off time the Brain drafts three candidate journal prompts — the trade most deviated from plan, the one best-executed, the emotional moment between. He approves any, edits any, discards any. Entries attach to trades automatically.

Why: the difference between a good trader and a great one is a filled journal. The Brain lowers the cost of filling one to zero.

N·06 Weekly
Your edge moved this week. Quietly.

Sunday afternoon, unprompted, once a week: a 4-line summary of the statistically significant changes in the trader’s edge vector. Which setup improved. Which decayed. Which habit correlates with the change. Dismissible. Savable. Exportable.

Why: edge decays silently. The Brain’s one responsibility is to make the silent audible.

F06 · XIII · THE ORB

Five states. One sigil. The Brain’s face.

visual grammar

The Brain has a physical identity on screen — a single, living orb that rests in the bottom-right of every page. It never screams. It never blinks. It breathes. Its colour tells the trader what state the Brain is in, before any word is written. It is the visual grammar of availability, attention, and silence.

THE SIGIL
A breathing indicator of presence, not a button.

The orb is never more than 28 pixels in diameter at rest. It rotates three concentric rings at different speeds, each ring mapped to a layer of the context stack. When the Brain is listening, the inner core glows and a fourth ring appears. When it’s thinking, the rings pulse in rhythm. When it has refused, the core dims.

The orb is not a prompt. Tapping it does not trigger the console — only a keystroke, a wake word, or a long-press does. The orb exists to tell the trader the Brain is alive, without interrupting him. It is a heartbeat, not a doorbell.

Rest Listening Thinking Replying Refusing
listen recall act see
F06 · XIV · INPUT MATRIX

Six ways into the Brain. Same reply, same log, same citation.

06 inputs

Traders are not typists. A trader at a desk will shout at the mic. A trader on a plane will type. A trader in a meeting will paste a screenshot. A trader on the subway will long-press. Every one of those six inputs routes to the same reasoning and produces the same cited answer. The Brain does not care how you asked.

Text

Keyboard in the command bar. Markdown-aware, intent-parsed, autocompletes on mentor names and instruments. Works on every surface, online or offline.

Paste or drop a screenshot — Discord, TradingView, a research chart, a photo of a whiteboard. The Brain OCRs it, identifies any traders in it, and resolves to records it can cite.

⌘ V · paste
Screen

No input at all — the Brain reads the page the trader is on. Ask “what am I looking at” and get an answer framed in the pixels actually on screen. Privacy flag per page.

“what is this”

Drop a PDF, CSV, XLSX, audio, or video. The Brain parses, summarises, extracts, compares. Cited against the trader’s history. Cloud lane opt-in for long docs.

drag · drop
Gesture

On mobile, long-press the orb to summon, three-finger tap to recall last reply, swipe-right to pin a view. On desktop, trackpad-force-touch on any citation jumps to source.

F06 · XVII · TEAM MODE

Four traders. One Brain session. Same log.

shared session

A prop desk, a mentor’s live call, a two-trader partnership — all of them need the Brain to be a shared console, not a personal one. Team Mode lets up to twelve named participants join a single session. Every ask is attributed. Every reply is visible to all. Every action is logged under the person who clicked. Privacy at the person level; cohesion at the session level.

TEAM MODE · LIVE
One session, many hands, one log.

A mentor opens a Brain session on his live call. Four students join. Any of them can summon the Brain with ⌘ K. The question shows under their name. The answer appears for everyone. Anyone can fork the answer into their own private workspace and keep iterating.

The Brain never blurs attribution. Every prompt, every reply, every citation is tagged with the participant who initiated it. The mentor can mute a participant, elevate a participant to co-driver, or lock the session to view-only. All actions are logged.

  • ATTRIBUTION · every ask tagged to its asker
  • FORKING · any reply → private workspace, in one tap
  • ROLES · owner, co-driver, participant, observer
  • PRIVACY · personal edge data never joined across members
  • RECORD · session log exportable as a signed transcript

F06 · XVIII · ERROR STATES

When the Brain fails. How it fails. What it says.

06 error modes

Every product fails. The Brain is designed to fail visibly, safely, and with a useful fallback. Below, the six most common error states the trader may encounter, the exact message shown, the human reason, and the fallback the Brain offers. Nothing is silently broken. Nothing is silently retried.

NO SOURCE ERR · 401
The Brain cannot find a citation.
I don’t have that. Closest match differs in 3 fields. I won’t paraphrase.

The answer would require inventing a source. The Brain is not allowed to do that under any circumstance.

FALLBACK: offers a widened search, a manual lookup, or a “create a record” CTA.
COOLDOWN ERR · 429
The Brain refuses to act during a self-imposed gate.
You set a 22-minute cooldown at 14:03. 11 minutes remaining. No ticket staged. No alert armed.

The trader’s own gate is active. The Brain honours it even when the trader changes his mind.

FALLBACK: lets the trader override with a logged acknowledgement, or journal instead.
CROSS-ROOM ERR · 403
The Brain will not read across rooms or seats.
That record lives in a room you don’t belong to. I can’t cross enclave boundaries.

Each room is a cryptographic enclave. The refusal is structural, not policy-level.

FALLBACK: offers to request access from the room owner, with one tap.
OFFLINE ERR · 0
The Brain lost network and degraded to local lanes.
No signal. Local lanes active: nav, vision, recall, journal. Cloud lanes queued.

The Brain auto-detects disconnect and continues with every lane that doesn’t require cloud.

FALLBACK: queued asks auto-resume on reconnect, in order, with user confirmation.
AMBIGUITY ERR · 300
The Brain can’t choose between two interpretations.
Two meanings fit: (a) last 5 NAS tickets; (b) last 5 NAS alerts. Which?

Guessing would give the wrong answer. Asking is two seconds and always the right call.

FALLBACK: presents both interpretations as inline chips; one tap commits.
OUT OF DOMAIN ERR · 418
The Brain is not a generalist.
That’s outside my domain. I don’t answer questions about restaurants, weather, or celebrities.

The Brain is trained on a trading lexicon, not the open web. Pretending otherwise would break every other promise.

FALLBACK: offers to hand-off to a general assistant of the trader’s choice (opt-in).
F06 · XIX · A DAY WITH THE BRAIN

A single Tuesday, hour by hour, spoken in the Brain’s voice.

09 moments

The best way to understand a product is to stand next to someone who uses it. Below, a slice of one Tuesday in the life of a full-time trader using the Brain. No feature invented for the narrative — every line below maps to a scenario, shortcut, or nudge already specified in this section.

TUESDAY · LONDON “Seat #412 · 4-year vet” 09 moments
05:58 WAKE The Brain is silent. He opens his phone. The orb breathes. He taps ⌘ K. “Brain, what am I walking into today?” The Brain returns: three events, one instrument he underperforms on, one mentor already posted, one of his own rules likely to be tested.
06:30 MENTOR Luke goes live. The Brain records the call with consent. By 07:48 — one minute after the call ends — the Brain has six clip-drafts ready for Luke, and a “Luke just spoke on your NAS ticket” whisper waiting for the trader.
08:12 REVIEW He asks “what did I lose yesterday and why?” — 180ms later, the full anatomy (trades, rule breaches, macro context, mentor notes) appears in a single view, pinned by his last tap.
09:42 NUDGE He drafts a ticket that would break rule R2. The Brain intercepts once, shows the rule, the violation, and a single override button. He revises. The ticket goes live, sized correctly.
11:04 VISION A friend sends a Discord screenshot he can’t place. He pastes it into the Brain. “That’s Mentor K.B., Scholar Room, 11 days ago. Not in your subs. His 90-day record on this call: 7W 3L.”
13:26 CRISIS He’s down 3R. He says “I want to make it back.” The Brain refuses to stage a ticket, opens a 22-minute circuit breaker, and surfaces his own rule R2 back at him. Mentor gets a silent ping (pre-consented). Trader steps away. Comes back clear.
16:18 BUILD He types “split my Sharpe London vs NY, 12 months.” The Brain builds the view in place — two curves, two tables, two regimes. He pins it. One tap exports a copy to his accountant in a template saved three months ago.
21:00 JOURNAL His declared cut-off. The Brain drafts three candidate journal entries: the most deviated trade, the best-executed, the emotional moment between. He edits one, approves three, discards none.
23:42 SILENCE The orb breathes. The Brain is not asking him anything. It never does. The last line in his audit log tonight: “trader · export · session transcript · SHA-256 signed.” He closes the laptop.

F06 · THE BRAIN · SEALED

Not a sidebar. Not a chatbot. Not a Jarvis. A console that navigates, sees, identifies, builds, recalls, acts, teaches, and remembers — for a trader, a mentor, a student, and a desk — with a citation on every claim, a log on every action, and a last-click on every execution.

— Archio Brain
Feature 06 · v0.6.2

Recap · the eight powers at a glance

  1. Summon Anywhere. ⌘K on any page, “Brain” on any mic. 180ms to open, 80ms to reply. Never interrupts an order in flight.
  2. Navigate by Intent. No menus. Ask for a page, a tab, a filter, a mentor call timestamp — arrive there with state pre-applied.
  3. See the Screen. The Brain reads pixels. Ask “what am I looking at” on any page and get an answer framed in what is actually there.
  4. Identify Anyone, Anything. Faces, handles, screenshots, patterns, instruments. Resolve to a verified record, with a citation.
  5. Build a Page in Place. Generative views — chart, table, matrix, overlay, heatmap — constructed inside the trader’s dashboard on the fly.
  6. Recall with Receipts. Every answer cites trade, call timestamp, mentor post, rule. No source, no answer — the Brain is honest.
  7. Act Inside Rails. Draft tickets, set alerts, prep journal entries, export bundles. The trader always clicks the last button.
  8. Teach From His Own Data. Concepts, mistakes, edges — explained using the trader’s own history, not generic lessons.

10.M Monetization Architecture

The ledger of who pays, who earns, and why.

A product that brings order to the mentor-and-student economy cannot fund itself with a generic SaaS pricing page. The monetization of Archio is a system, not a price list. It answers three questions the industry has never answered together: what the retail trader pays today for the broken stack; what subscription tiers replace that stack with a single bill; and how mentors earn, on rails we built, either through a variable revenue-share or a flat platform licence — their choice.

Model mix

Frontier-class for verdicts, cited scenarios, replay narration. Cheap-frontier for digests, journal distillation, routine Q&A. The Gateway routes dynamically based on stake.

Buffer

Every tier carries a 30% inference buffer above the modelled active-user load, absorbed before any overage is charged. We pad the room, not the invoice.

Overage

If a user blows past their tier budget, the copilot degrades to cheap-frontier automatically and prompts a token pack, rather than silently billing. No surprise invoices.

Why not $29

At $29/mo with 15k tokens, gross margin is <85% after support, infra, and Stripe fees. That does not fund frontier models, research, or the build quality we are insisting on. We would rather be honest about the cost than shave the model.

MON · IV · MENTOR LADDER

The mentor ladder. 33% up to 50%, or a flat licence.

4 rungs

A mentor comes to Archio with an audience. We give him the entire platform — room, calls, Forge, copilot, alumni graph — in exchange for a revenue share on his subscriptions processed on Archio’s rails. The share is performance-indexed: mentors who produce measurable student outcomes pay less. Mentors who ship a clean cohort move down the ladder, not up. The alternative: pay the flat T4 Mentor licence and keep 100% of subscription revenue. His choice, reviewed quarterly.

MON · V · PAYMENT FLOW

How the money moves. Five steps. Stripe Connect.

5 steps

Every subscription, every call, every token pack, every milestone bonus settles through Archio’s Stripe Connect rail. Funds are held escrow-style by Archio at charge time and disbursed to the mentor’s Connect account on the published schedule. Transparent. Daily. Audited.

RAIL · STRIPE CONNECT
Student card → Archio platform → Mentor Connect
01 · Charge
Student subscribes.

The student authorises the card on Archio. Stripe customer created under Archio; subscription object created against the mentor’s price.

02 · Escrow
Held by Archio.

Funds land in the platform account. Refund window honoured (7-day money-back). No disbursement yet.

03 · Compute
Share calculated.

Mentor rung is looked up live. Share applied. Stripe fees & taxes deducted from the mentor’s portion transparently.

04 · Payout
Daily to mentor.

Mentor’s share is pushed via Stripe Connect transfers, daily, to his linked bank. Payout receipt is a first-class Archio object.

05 · Bonus
Graduate milestone.

When a student hits a graduation milestone (O·04), the graduate bonus is disbursed separately, with its own receipt and alumni graph update.

MON · VI · BUSINESS LOGIC

Six cells of policy. Plain language. No hidden clauses.

6 policies

Everything the industry obfuscates with a 14-page ToS, in six cells. These are the business-logic decisions every user sees before they pay.

P · 01
14-day full trial on every paid tier.

Not a limited trial — full capability. Trade Forge, copilot, Mentor Dashboard, all of it. The card is authorised but not charged. Cancel inside 14 days and pay nothing.

P · 02
Pause anytime, downgrade anytime.

A trader away on holiday, or in a losing-streak cooldown, can pause his subscription for up to 60 days a year. Plan data, history, journal, and rules are retained in full. Dignity before revenue.

P · 03
Annual = two months free.

Annual billing returns a 17% discount across every tier — effectively two months free. For the Trader tier that is $350 in annual savings; for Mentor · Room, it is $1,000; for Institute, $2,000. Same features, fewer invoices, better planning.

P · 04
Prop firm & broker co-funding.

Select prop firms and brokers co-fund their traders’ Archio subscriptions. A funded trader on FTMO can receive the Trader tier on the firm’s account. The incentive is aligned: firm wants disciplined traders.

P · 05
Founding 500 · locked pricing.

The first 500 Trader subscribers receive $125/mo for life (instead of $175) and the first 100 Mentor · Room subscribers receive $375/mo for life (instead of $500). Locked as long as they remain subscribed. A single, transparent founding cohort. No tiered grandfathering games.

P · 06
Tokens never expire while subscribed.

Unused monthly token budget rolls forward up to 3x the tier’s monthly grant. Purchased token packs never expire. We do not profit from forgotten balances.

F · MONETIZATION
Subscriptions buy the surface. Tokens buy the depth. Mentors earn on rails.

Five tiers (three mentor variants), a published AI cost ledger, one token economy, a four-rung mentor ladder, and a Stripe Connect rail that settles daily. The fragmented $410–$820 stack becomes one subscription from $95, the professional trader’s cockpit is $175, and the mentor economy acquires the first revenue-share that is indexed to student outcomes.

12 What This Means For Institutions

Prop firms. Brokers. Hedge funds. Banks.

The retail trader is the product's first customer. He is not the product's only constituent. The same structure that gives him order gives the institutions around him something they have never had before: a legible, audited, behaviorally-observed retail layer. This is the part of the landing page that allocators will read quietly while the trader is scrolling.

Institution · 01 Proprietary Trading Firms

The funded trader model is the single greatest alignment of interest retail finance has ever seen. It is also the most structurally lonely. A trader who passes an evaluation is handed a capital allocation and a payout agreement and left alone in his bedroom. He fails, on average, not because he cannot trade — he passed an evaluation — but because there is no infrastructure around him at the moment he starts to lose.

Archio gives prop firms the first real retention layer. A trader embedded in Archio has his psychology monitored, his edge tracked, his mentor agent available 24/7, and a dashboard the firm can optionally see. The failure rate goes down. The payout rate goes up. The firm's capital is safer. Every prop firm in the world should want its traders inside Archio.

For firms: integration is a single line. The trader brings his own funded account; Archio reads the feed. The firm gets a dashboard of aggregate behavioral risk, fully anonymized, across its entire trader base. This is the first time a prop firm has ever been able to see its population.

Institution · 02 Brokerages & Exchanges

Retail brokerages compete on spread, leverage, and speed. None of them compete on keeping the trader alive, because none of them have the infrastructure to. A trader who blows his account is the broker's second-worst customer, right behind a trader who opens an account and never funds it.

Archio is the only product an honest broker can recommend to its clients without reservation. The broker does not lose revenue to Archio; Archio increases the average account lifetime, which increases the lifetime revenue of every account. We expect broker partnerships to become one of the default distribution channels for Archio by year three.

Institution · 03 Hedge Funds & Allocators

Every serious allocator has wondered, quietly, whether the behavioral signals in retail trading could be turned into an alpha-extraction layer. They could not, before, because retail trading was a statistical noise field — a billion uncorrelated decisions with no metadata. Archio is the first product to annotate retail behavior at the psychological level in real time.

At scale, the platform will produce the first audited, anonymized dataset of trader psychology, decision behavior, and capitulation timing on record. Whether that dataset is ever offered externally is a decision we are not prepared to make today. What we are prepared to say is that its existence will be the most valuable behavioral finance corpus in the history of retail markets.

For allocators: Archio is also a window into the sophistication gradient of retail, which is the largest single behavioral sentiment indicator we have never had.

Institution · 04 Retail Banks & Neo-banks

Banks have spent a decade watching their younger customers move uninvested cash into brokerages they do not own. The loss of deposit share is structural, not cyclical. It will not reverse by lowering a fee. It will only reverse when the bank has something worth keeping the customer for.

A bank that integrates Archio — via API, via co-branded surface, or via acquisition — gives its customer base the first professional-grade trading environment that is not a standalone brokerage. The bank retains the deposit relationship and gives its customer a reason to stop logging into three separate products.

Institution · 05 Regulators & the Public Interest

Retail trading regulation is a loud argument conducted with almost no data. Nobody knows, empirically, what fraction of retail losses come from bad mechanics, bad psychology, or bad actors. Archio, at scale, knows. We are committed to making aggregated, anonymized behavioral findings available to regulators in jurisdictions that work with us in good faith.

The future of retail trading does not have to be a consumer protection fight. It can be an infrastructure upgrade. Archio is how that upgrade begins.

“The retail floor has been run like a carnival for fifty years. We are not here to close it. We are here to turn it into a city.”

— Institutional positioning memo

The first-time reader — his pulse, in order.

We do not prescribe colour. We prescribe somatic intent. If you deliver a direction and a trader's body does these six things in these six beats, you have done the job. If the body does them in a different order, re-cut. If the body does nothing, start over.

  1. T + 00:00 Land
    Recognition

    He reads the hook. His shoulders drop by a centimetre. He thinks: "Someone has seen my desk." No scroll yet. Stillness.

    DO give him one sentence, typeset with authority, centered, and the air to breathe around it. DO NOT float anything.

  2. T + 00:05 Mirror
    Relief

    He sees his eleven tabs drawn back at him. He thinks: "They named it." His jaw unclenches. He scrolls for the first time.

    DO make the mess feel accurate, not cartoonish. DO NOT cute-ify the fragmentation.

  3. T + 00:18 Collapse
    Revelation

    He watches the eleven tabs collapse into one brain. He thinks: "This could actually be possible." His breath shortens for a moment — then lengthens.

    DO earn this moment. It is the one piece of motion the page may spend. DO NOT repeat it anywhere else.

  4. T + 00:42 Feel
    Agency

    He meets the three interactive demos. He thinks: "I can touch this." He picks one. He touches it. He plays with it.

    DO let him succeed with his first interaction. DO NOT gate anything behind a sign-up.

  5. T + 01:30 Place
    Belonging

    He meets the three paths — Learning, Growing, Leading — and sees himself in one of them. He thinks: "That is me." He clicks.

    DO write the path for him, not at him. DO NOT market — diagnose.

  6. T + 02:00 Decide
    Conviction

    He reaches the CTA. He thinks: "I already know what I'm doing with this." He clicks without theatrics. He does not need to be sold to. He is already in.

    DO give him one single button. DO NOT give him three. The choice was made thirty seconds ago.

What every direction refuses.

Colour is yours. Type is yours. Rhythm is yours. These four refusals are not. They survive every direction because they describe the reader's body, not a taste.

No SaaS boilerplate.
If a sentence could appear on a B2B landing page for anything else in the world, cut it. The trader has been marketed to his whole life. The page must read like an author wrote it — not a growth team.
No “AI sparkle”.
No rainbow gradients. No glowing orbs. No “now with AI” badges. The intelligence of the product is demonstrated by behaviour, not decoration. If the page screams AI, we have already lost.
No panic motion.
Nothing snaps. Nothing bounces. Nothing pulses for attention. The page knows the reader is reading. Motion is reserved for moments of meaning — the collapse in Chapter 11, the copilot card, and perhaps one more. That is all.
Forbidden words.
Revolutionary. Best-in-class. Game-changing. Seamless. Empower. Unlock your potential. Leverage. Ecosystem. Cutting-edge. Synergy. Disrupt. Next-gen. Anything that begins with “Imagine if…”. These words are banned not because they are ugly but because they are someone else's vocabulary, and this page is not someone else.

“Design is not the decoration of the brief. Design is the brief. If the reader's pulse does the six things, the colour did its job.”

— Uykan Kadric & Luke Callahan, to the studio
