The grid, across all pages

A single 12-column grid. 96px gutters at desktop, 24px gutters at mobile. Maximum content width 960px for reading sections; full-bleed for cinematic sections (the break, the shoulder, the promise). Vertical rhythm is a 24px baseline; every section starts and ends on a multiple of that. Type aligns to cap-height, not to box. These are rules, not suggestions.

Density, section by section

Reading density varies by section type. The hook is sparse: one sentence per screen. The outcomes and platform index are dense: five to ten lines per screen. The feature pages alternate — two paragraphs, then a trio of cards, then a list of submodules, then a single line, then the next. The reader should feel the page breathing in and out.

§
15 The Institutional Lens

Why a hedge fund, a prop firm, a broker, and a bank all want this page to exist.

Retail traders are the buyers on the landing page. They are not the only readers. A landing page of this weight is also read by the people who allocate capital, route flow, and write cheques — and a landing page that reads well to a 22-year-old at a prop firm desk must also read well to a 52-year-old at an allocation committee. This chapter is about who else is at the table, and what they are looking for when they scroll. The design must not speak to them directly; it must simply not contradict what they are quietly checking for.

The hedge fund allocator.

He is not our customer, but he is our ambient audience. He reads the page the way he reads any new infrastructure piece — looking for four signals. First, that the problem being named is the real problem (he knows what tilt looks like in his own book). Second, that the solution is not a wrapper around a model he has already seen ten times this year. Third, that the language of the founders is the language of someone who has sat through drawdown. Fourth, that the data architecture — the thing in chapter sixteen — actually survives a procurement review.

He will not buy from us. He will refer an emerging manager in his network to us, or recommend us to a family office considering a retail education play. The landing page is the diligence document he reads before making that referral. It has to answer, silently, the questions he would ask if he were on our board.

The prop firm operator.

He has a thousand funded traders and a washout problem. His retention curve has a cliff at week six, the week his average trader blows a challenge or tilts a funded account. Every retention tool on the market is a warning email. He needs the thing on this landing page, because the thing on this landing page is an intervention. The moment the Cortex says STOP before a revenge trade is the moment his washout number drops.

When he reads the page, he is counting two things. How fast his traders can adopt it — is the onboarding less than ten minutes? — and whether the psychology layer can be surfaced to him without crossing the line into surveillance. He wants aggregate patterns on his floor, not individual dossiers. The page must suggest the answer is yes on both counts without turning into a B2B site.

What he sees today

A dashboard that tells him which traders are drawing down after the drawdown has happened. A compliance layer that flags losses, never their cause. A relationship where he is either absent or intrusive. No middle ground.

What Archio gives him

A floor-level view of which psychological patterns are active on which desks, in real time, with the individual trader's privacy preserved. The ability to offer his traders a tool they would have paid for themselves — and are grateful he covered. A retention lift he can write in his next fundraise.

The broker.

His incentives are the ugliest in the chain. He makes money when his clients trade, and he makes more money when his clients trade poorly. Every serious person in the industry knows this, and every serious person in the industry pretends otherwise. A broker who partners with Archio is, publicly, choosing to be on the side of his clients at the cost of a measurable percentage of his flow. That is a branding event, not a partnership. It lets him say something that almost no broker has been able to say credibly in the last twenty years: we want you to still be here next year.

The landing page should leave space for brokers to see themselves in it. Not with logos — logos are cheap. With a quiet signal, somewhere in the footer or the platform index, that execution routes through real accounts at real brokers, and that the platform's incentives are aligned with the client's longevity. One line. That is enough.

The private bank and the family office.

They do not trade themselves, but they staff desks that do, and they increasingly have mandates to understand the behaviour of principals who self-direct a slice of their own wealth. A managing director at a private bank is not going to put Archio in front of a client directly — but he is going to read the landing page when it gets forwarded to him by a nephew or a VP at a corporate client who has started trading on the side. The landing page has to clear the bar of institutional taste. No exclamation points. No promises. No crypto-adjacent aesthetic. Just clarity, restraint, and the air of a firm that knows what it is doing.

The press.

A landing page of this scope becomes a primary source for a Financial Times profile, a Bloomberg feature, a podcast preamble. The copy must be quotable. Every headline in this brief is a sentence a reporter could lift and paste into a piece without attribution and it would still read as a thesis. The design must photograph well — the two or three hero moments must hold up as still images in a 1200-word article. The page is not just a conversion surface; it is the reference image of the company for the next decade.

§
16 Data Architecture

What the system sees, and what it will never see.

The landing page will never publish an architecture diagram. It will, however, be read by people who can tell within thirty seconds whether the people who built the product understand what they are talking about. This chapter is the substrate the copy stands on. It is written so that if a reader asks a clarifying question in an email — and we expect them to — the answer is already here.

The three data surfaces.

Archio captures, reasons over, and responds to three data surfaces. Nothing else. Together they produce every intervention, every decomposition, every coach card the product has ever issued.

01 · Execution data.
Every order ticket the trader submits, every fill he receives, every cancellation, every modification. Time, price, size, pair, account, broker, session. The raw cadence of the book. Ingested through broker APIs where available, through a lightweight connector where it is not, never through screenshots. Latency: sub-second.
02 · Behavioural data.
How the trader interacted with the platform in the ninety seconds before, during, and after each trade. How long he hovered on the ticket. How many times he changed the size. Whether the trade followed a loss, a win, a break. Whether he opened the chart, the journal, the community before pulling the trigger. The cognitive residue of the act.
03 · Narrative data.
What the trader said about the trade — in the journal, in the chat, in the morning prep, in the post-mortem. His own words, structured by prompts, weighted by the AI, cross-referenced with the execution and behavioural surfaces. The trader writes a paragraph and the system finds the pattern.

The three it will never capture.

We have decided, and will publish, the boundary. This is the clearest possible line between what a supervisory AI and a surveillance AI do.

× · Biometrics.
No heart rate. No eye tracking. No camera. No microphone. No keystroke timing beyond the order form itself. If you cannot infer the state from what the trader has chosen to type or click, you do not infer it. The body is off-limits.
× · Cross-app signals.
No browser history. No clipboard scraping. No screenshots of other windows. No reading of messages from apps Archio does not own. If a pattern cannot be seen inside Archio, the system does not try to see it.
× · Third-party telemetry.
No selling of behavioural data to brokers, prop firms, or data brokers of any kind. Ever. The product exists because traders trust us with their losses; the moment that trust is monetised outside the room, the product does not exist.

“The AI sees what he types, what he trades, and what he writes. Nothing else. That is enough.”

How the three surfaces talk.

Execution data enters the Forge. Behavioural data enters the Cortex. Narrative data enters the Journal. Each surface is independently useful. The product becomes supernormal at the intersections. The Cortex flags a revenge pattern because the behavioural surface said "he sized up ninety seconds after a loss" and the execution surface said "the ticket is already on the book" and the narrative surface said "he wrote yesterday that he wanted to get the money back by Friday." No single signal is enough. Three are.

The model stack, in one paragraph.

A stack, not a model. A classifier detects the pattern class. A ranker scores its severity against the trader's own history. A retriever pulls the closest past episode. A generator writes the coach card in language that has already been approved by the trader's chosen voice. Each layer can be audited independently, each output is shown with its citations, and the trader can always see why the system said what it said. The word "hallucination" does not survive contact with this stack, because nothing is ever generated without something to cite.

Privacy, posture-level.

Every trader's data belongs to him. He can export it in one click. He can delete it in one click. The mentor sees only what the trader has chosen to share. The community sees only what the trader has chosen to post. The founders do not read private journals. Aggregate analytics — “how many traders tilted this week” — are computed without joining back to individuals. This is not a marketing posture. It is the only posture that lets the product keep working.

§
17 Trust & Governance

The rules we wrote before we needed them.

Every platform eventually meets the moment where a user is hurt by something it did or failed to do. The platforms that survive that moment are the ones that published their rules before the moment arrived. This chapter is our rulebook. The landing page does not show it in full. It shows the trader a version of it, where it matters, in a language he can read.

The Mentor Covenant.

Every mentor on the platform signs one document before the first student pays. It is one page long. It forbids five things — screenshotted win photos without full-trade context, guaranteed results of any kind, affiliate links to unregulated brokers, private paid signals outside the platform, and any recruitment of students into off-platform chats for monetary purposes. It requires two things — a public track record and a published teaching philosophy. A mentor who breaks the covenant is removed. The covenant is reprinted in full on every mentor's profile page, in the footer of every community he runs, and in the onboarding of every student who joins him. The system does not let him hide it.

The Copilot Covenant.

The AI will never tell a trader to take a specific trade. It will never tell him to size specifically. It will never tell him what the market will do. It will surface patterns, cite sources, ask questions, flag behaviours, and coach him toward his own decision. The trader is the decision-maker and the AI is the supervisor, and the product is built to make that boundary obvious in every piece of UI. The landing page must not blur this line. Every description of the copilot must use verbs of support, never verbs of instruction. Intercept, classify, flag, ask, surface, decompose, coach. Never decide, never recommend a trade, never tell you when to enter.

The Community Covenant.

No one can post a win without the system attaching the trade's full context — entry, exit, R, timeframe, session, whether a rule was broken. No one can DM a minor. No one can offer paid services inside a public room without the mentor flag. No one can run a challenge. No one can sell an indicator without publishing the code. The goal is not restriction; it is the removal of the asymmetric-information pressure that makes retail rooms feel like casinos. The page must show that the room is calm because the rules are clear.

The Archio Covenant.

The thing we promise back to the user, in exchange for his trust. We will not sell his data. We will not run ads against his trading. We will not make our money from his volume. We will not accept paid placement from mentors. We will not introduce partners we would not recommend to our own brothers. We will show our own founders' trades on the platform — wins, losses, tilt episodes included — so that nothing the system asks of the user is something it does not first ask of us.

“Four covenants. One page each. Written before the first user signed up.”

How the landing page carries all this without saying all of it.

Trust is carried by restraint. If the page does not over-promise, the reader does not need to see the full covenant to believe that one exists. The words we are willing to use tell the reader as much as the words we are willing to publish in a legal document. The design should use the restraint of the copy as a trust signal: the absence of exclamation points is a signal; the absence of testimonial sliders is a signal; the absence of a countdown timer is a signal. The reader who has been on this side of the industry for years will feel it in the first three seconds, and he is the reader we are writing for.

§
18 The First One Thousand

Who this page is really written for, at launch.

A landing page written for everyone is a landing page read by no one. The page is written for the first one thousand traders who will ever read it — because those thousand will set the culture of the platform for its next hundred thousand. If the page attracts the right thousand, the next ninety-nine thousand will arrive already shaped. If it attracts the wrong thousand, we will spend the following two years trying to remove them.

The profile.

He is between twenty-four and forty. He has been trading, seriously, for between eighteen months and six years. He has lost an amount of money that genuinely hurt him at least once and he is no longer telling his friends about his winners. He still has the scars of his worst trade accessible in conversation. He has paid, and regretted paying, for at least one course or signal group. He does not call himself a trader at parties yet. He works at it every morning before his day job or full-time from a quiet room in the flat he rents.

When he reads the landing page, he is not looking for permission to trade. He is looking for permission to trust again — the product, the community, his own discipline. The page is written to give him that permission honestly, by not asking for too much, too fast.

What he is not.

He is not a hobbyist. He is not new. He is not a YouTube viewer who watched a reel on "prop firm strategies." He is not someone who thinks of the market as a gambling venue. He is not anti-psychology. He is not anti-AI. He is not anti-mentor, but he is allergic to guru-coded aesthetics. He is not impressed by lambos, Bali rooftops, or green-candle backdrops.

The Reddit and the Discord where he already lives.

There is a canonical set of places on the internet where this man spends his mornings. Certain subreddits — the quiet ones, where posts are deleted for being promotional. Certain Discord servers — the invite-only ones with fewer than a thousand members, where a post is a paragraph, not a screenshot. A handful of X accounts with five thousand followers each who trade institutional size without saying so. He respects these places because they have, against all odds, stayed clean. Our landing page must read like something that was made by someone who has been in those rooms and, for his own reasons, has stopped expecting anyone else to build for them. If the page reads like that, he forwards it to three friends inside the hour. If it does not, he does not send it to anyone.

The tone of our acquisition.

We do not run paid acquisition on the landing page at launch. There is no budget for Meta ads. The first thousand arrive because the page was posted by a respected account, screenshotted by a thoughtful account, or forwarded by a friend whose taste they trust. The page is the ad. The page has to be embarrassable to send — in the positive sense. It has to make the sender look like someone with taste.

The second thousand and beyond.

The second thousand will come through mentors. The third through prop firms. The fourth through brokers who want their better clients to stay alive longer. The fifth through a feature in a major publication. By the time the twentieth thousand arrives, the page will have been redesigned twice, but the shape of this first version — the restraint, the density, the warmth of the grammar — will still be visible in every later version. Like the first flag of a country. You can always tell.

§
19 The Moat

Why this is difficult to copy, and why that shows in the design.

Every serious product has a question a serious reader asks in his head: "Why can't someone else just build this?" The landing page does not answer that question out loud — an answer out loud would sound defensive — but it has to be built by people who know the answer, because the answer shapes every choice on the page.

01 · Integrated emotional data.

Any team with six months and a funded seed round can build a charting front-end. Two teams can build a journaling app in a weekend. A well-staffed AI team can build a pattern classifier in a month. What no team can build quickly is the corpus of paired trades and trader narratives that lets a model learn the specific shape of tilt — because that corpus does not exist on the open internet and it does not exist inside a broker's data warehouse. It only gets built inside a platform where the trader types his own sentence next to his own trade. Every trader who joins Archio and writes one journal entry makes the system a little better for the next. The moat compounds. The landing page does not claim this, but the design carries the weight of it.

02 · Permission.

A broker cannot build this product because the broker has the wrong incentive — no serious trader believes the company making money from his volume is the company best placed to tell him to stop. A charting platform cannot build this product because it has spent fifteen years training its users to associate it with charts, not psychology. A prop firm cannot build this product because its business is selling challenges, not extending careers. The only team that can build this product is a team that has chosen, deliberately, not to pick up any of those easier business models. That is a moat made of restraint, not technology. It shows in the landing page as the things the page refuses to do.

03 · Taste.

There is a reason the great consumer products of the last twenty years — the ones that made categories rather than competed in them — all look like they were made by small teams with strong preferences. Taste is difficult to clone because it is an accumulation of ten thousand small choices, each of them arguable, and most of them impossible to defend in a spreadsheet. A competitor can copy our features within a year. He cannot copy the feeling of the footer. He cannot copy the particular absence of an exclamation point. He cannot copy the way our three demos sit on the page. He cannot, most of all, copy the fact that the page reads like it was written by a trader who was up at four in the morning, for someone else who was up at four in the morning. That is what we are selling.

04 · Ecosystem lock.

The Forge sits on top of the broker connectors we have wired. The Psychology OS sits on top of the behavioural data the Forge emits. The Dashboard sits on top of the narrative the Journal captures. The Network sits on top of the mentor covenants we have already collected. Each module makes the next module more valuable, and each is less interesting on its own than with its neighbours. A competitor entering the market from the side will have to rebuild all four simultaneously, and the person who tries that is not going to beat us; he is going to release a worse version of each of them and quietly pivot.

05 · First flag.

The first mover in a category does not always win, but the first mover who gets the category name right almost always does. "Trading OS" is the language we plant. Every competitor who arrives afterward will be measured against a phrase we wrote. The landing page is the document that plants that flag. Design accordingly.

“Taste is the only moat that does not erode. Everything else is a head start.”

§
20 Delivery & Cadence

Four phases. Clear ownership.

This brief does not specify a calendar, because calendars are a negotiation between us. It specifies the shape of the work. Four phases. Each one ends with a single artefact that we sign, named below. We expect a named delivery lead on QCLAY's side. We provide a named founder on ours.

  1. Phase 01 — Architecture. Sitemap, wireframes for the landing and every feature page, section weighting agreed. Artefact: a single PDF of greybox wireframes with our annotations approved. Owner: QCLAY lead. Reviewer: founders.
  2. Phase 02 — Surface. Visual design for the landing page and one feature page (we suggest Psychology OS, because it is the hardest). Full type, palette, motion language established. Artefact: two Figma files (landing + one feature page), fully specced, ready for engineering. Owner: QCLAY art direction. Reviewer: founders.
  3. Phase 03 — Extension. The remaining four feature pages (Network, Forecast, Forge, Dashboard AI), each brought to parity with the Psychology OS template. The Feel It demos are specced in motion prototypes. Artefact: five feature page Figmas + motion prototypes. Owner: QCLAY + founders co-driving copy. Reviewer: founders.
  4. Phase 04 — Fabrication. Engineering handoff. Every asset exported, every breakpoint specced, every interaction documented. Archio engineering builds. QCLAY stands by for QA on fidelity. Artefact: live staging URL, founder-signed. Owner: Archio engineering. Reviewer: QCLAY + founders.

What we sign off on, and when.

We sign off at four moments only: end of Phase 01 (architecture), end of Phase 02 (visual language), end of Phase 03 (extension parity), and end of Phase 04 (live). No design-by-committee. No WhatsApp revisions. Every sign-off is documented in a single paragraph we both initial, and that paragraph is the contract for the next phase. Change requests outside of these four gates are tracked as a separate scope.

How we work during the phases.

One call per week, thirty minutes, standing. One shared Notion workspace with live commenting. One WhatsApp thread for urgent clarifications — always answered within the business day. No group calls unless requested. No Slack. QCLAY's lead has our phone numbers. We have his.

Headline
The copilot that intervenes.
Deck
The single reason a serious trader will pay for Archio.
Section 01 · Current experience (opening line)
Your worst trade last week happened between a thought and a click. Your platform did not see the thought. Your journal caught the click nine hours later. The thing in the middle — the ninety seconds — is where the money left, and no tool you own today was built to be there.
Section 02 · What Archio does here
A live over-the-shoulder AI that sees your psychology, your edge, and your execution in one surface. It does not ask you to journal afterwards. It is there during.
Section 03 · What makes it different
Four card labels: Live intervention · Five-stage flow · Neural topology · Cause-and-effect engine
Section 04 · How it connects
The Forge emits execution data. The journal emits narrative data. The Cortex is where they meet. Every other module reads from the Cortex.
Section 05 · Inside the feature (11 submodule labels)
Scan · Diagnose · Understand · Act · Track · Neural Topology · Emotion Chapters · Cause & Effect · Pattern Detection · Cooldown · Intervention Verdict
Section 06 · Who this is for
Not the trader who has never lost money. Not the trader who thinks he does not have a psychology. The trader who has a drawdown scar he can point to on the map of his last year.
Section 07 · CTA
Try the copilot on your last trade →

Pull quotes, reusable.

Any of these may be placed as a full-bleed pull quote in any section where the rhythm supports it. All are founder-approved.

“We are not building a better chart. We are building the floor under every chart.”

“A trader alone is a trader alone. A trader watched is a trader growing.”

“The best intervention is the one that happens before the trade, not after it.”

“Order is not the opposite of freedom. Order is what makes freedom repeatable.”

Words to borrow.

Intervene. Intercept. Lock. Surface. Cite. Coach. Route. Decompose. Compound. Repeat. Audit. Classify. Carry. Rebuild. Index. Memory. Floor. Surface. Signal. Silence. Pattern. Pressure. Discipline. Clarity. Structure. Order.

Words to refuse.

Revolutionary. Best-in-class. Game-changing. Unlock your potential. Next-generation. Supercharge. 10x. Unleash. Journey. Crushing it. Disruption. Synergy. AI-powered. Not for tone, but for principle. A page built to last ten years cannot afford any of these.

§
22 Closing

The standard we are building toward.

"The best work of our generation will be the work that brings order to a place that accepted its chaos for too long. Retail finance is that place. The landing page is the first room of that order."

— ArchioAI, 2026

The number of companies that have ever tried to do what we are asking QCLAY to help us do is zero. There is no precedent we can point you to, no reference site we can ask you to outdo, no competitor whose landing we want to beat. The standard we are building toward is not a benchmark; it is an absence. We want this page to be the thing future teams point to when they want to show a designer what "order" looks like on the open internet.

When it is done, it should feel the way a great novel feels in the first paragraph — not clever, not salesy, not trying; just confident that the author knows something the reader is about to find out. It should be quiet, dense, warm, and absolutely sure of itself. A reader should be able to linger on any single section of it for a full minute and not run out of something to read. A skeptical reader should close the tab and come back the next day because he was not done.

We believe that, built correctly, this page will still be the canonical example of its category ten years from now. Not because we will have been unchanged — the product will have evolved a hundred times — but because the shape of this first room will have set the shape of every room that followed. Structure is the most valuable thing a young category can inherit, and structure is what this document is about.

“Bend the spec. Do not bend the feeling.”

— The only line we insist on

Thank you for reading. Thank you for taking this seriously. We know what this page is worth and what we are paying for it, and we know that a trivially smaller brief would have been easier to write. We chose this length because the work deserves it. We trust you to do the same.
